items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

Economic Growth and Job Creation—Progress
1. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)  to the Minister of Finance : What steps is the
Government taking to support new jobs and build a productive and competitive
economy?
5880 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Oct 2012

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is entitled to ask a question. Before the
Minister has got a word out there were lots of interjections. That is not reasonable.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am pleased to get a question on jobs
today. I did not get one yesterday, so the crisis must be over. The Government has
worked through an economic programme to support business invest ment because it is
business investment that leads to more jobs. Specific measures include a 90-day trial
period and reducing company tax to 28 percen t. ACC levies have been reduced, saving
$600 million this year, we have removed 170 unnecessary and excessive regulations,
and, in terms of direct intervention on behalf of young people, we have the $152 million
Youth Opportunities package, which includes 4,000 places in Job Ops.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: How have the New Zealand economy and employment market
performed over the past 2 years, and what is the outlook for the next few years?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: A very good question. In net terms, almost 60,000 more
New Zealanders have jobs now than 2 years ago, and unemployment is forecast to fall.
That has happened because the economy grew  by 2.6 percent in the year to June, and
annual growth is forecast at between 2 and 3 percent over the next 4 years—better than
most developed countries. The after-tax av erage wage is up by 20 percent since 2008.
New Zealand now has the lowest inflation ra te since 1999, which means that the cost of
living is increasing at its slowest rate in 12 years. All of this will help support jobs.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What examples has he seen of jobs being created in the
infrastructure sector?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Through the recession the Government, despite tight
financial times, has maintained a consistently high level of investment in infrastructure.
Here are just a few examples of those proj ects: there will be a bout 1,000 construction
jobs on the new Wiri Prison, for which the contract has been signed, 1,000 new jobs
over the next 4 years at the height of the Waterview construc tion, and nearly 2,000
people employed in the roll-out  of ultra-fast broadband, whic h has been assisted with
$1.5 billion of investment by the Government.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What recent reports has he seen on jobs and output in the
manufacturing sector?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have seen reports that there is a crisis in jobs in the
manufacturing sector, and, as is often the case with what the Opposition parties say, that
is wrong. The household labour force survey shows that the number of people employed
in manufacturing has remained quite steady since the beginning of 2009, although it did
drop somewhat in the last 18 months of th e Labour Government’s time in office. The
number is now fluctuating between 245,000 and 255,000 people, depending on the
season. Over the past 2 years employment in manufacturing has actually gone up a
little, from 239,500 to 246,500. Manufacturing output , in GDP terms, has risen by 8
percent since June 2009. Latest GDP data shows the manufacturing sector growing by
2.5 percent over the last year.
Dotcom Case—Government Communications Security Bureau Staffing
2. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First)  to the Minister responsible
for the GCSB : Specifically, have there been st aff issues associated with the
Government Communications Security Bure au and Dotcom affair brought to his
attention by the Government Communications Security Bureau or members of the New
Zealand Police, in which such staff members no longer work in their previous capacity
for the Government Communications Security Bureau or any government agency; if so,
what were the circumstances?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The director of the
Government Communications Security Bureau has raised some staff issues with me. As
17 Oct 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5881
the member will be aware, the director made a public statement last week, which
advised that an investigation had commenced within the bureau as to whether there had
been unauthorised disclosure of information, and if so, its source. I do not believe that it
is appropriate for me to make further comment about staff matters, which are clearly the
responsibility of the director.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does the Prime Minister have any knowledge at all of
disciplinary action being taken against an  individual working for the Government
Communications Security Bureau in respect of the Dotcom affair; if so, why will he not
tell the House when he was first informed of it?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not in a position to disc uss staffing matters; they are a
matter for the director, and best left with him.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am not asking him to
discuss staffing matters; I am asking him wh ether there was a discussion relating to
staffing matters that came to his attention. That is a different question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am prepared to let the member repeat his question, but that was
not what his question actually asked. In cas e I am in error, I am happy for the member
to repeat his question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does he have any knowledge at all of disciplinary action
being taken against an individual work ing for the Government Communications
Security Bureau in respect of the Dotcom af fair; if so, why will he not tell the House
when he was first informed of it?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not in a position to conf irm whether disciplinary action
has or has not been taken. I am  advised by the director as he sees fit. But they are
ongoing staffing matters and it would be inappropriate for me to comment further.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Is the Minister saying that he  is not aware of a member of
the Government Communications Security Bu reau being specifically and particularly
put on “gardening leave” in respect of the Kim Dotcom affair, despite the name and role
of that person being widely known around Wellington?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What I am prepared to say is that any matters involving
personnel at the Government Communications  Security Bureau are a matter for the
director. It would be inappropriate for me to publicly comment on those at this time.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: In another case, can he assure the House that an officer of
the New Zealand Police force with a record  of 15 years’ service in the Diplomatic
Protection Squad never spoke to him about Dotcom prior to 19 January 2012, the date
the PM now finally admits he first learnt of Kim Dotcom?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have no recollection of any Diplomatic Protection Squad
agent speaking to me about that.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Is he saying as Minister that a member of the Prime
Minister’s protection squad w ith a record of 15 years’ service to Prime Ministers,
including himself, never told him as Prim e Minister of his in tention to leave the
Diplomatic Protection Squad to go to work for Kim Dotcom?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is referring to a chap whose last name I do not
know; his first name is Regan. He does not wo rk for the Diplomatic Protection Squad;
he works for—or he used to work for—th e VIP Protection Squad in Auckland, and, no,
I was not aware that he went to work for Kim Dotcom.
Dotcom Case—Briefings and Prime Minister’s Statements
3. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: Further
to his answers to the first supplementary  question to Oral Question No 1 on 26
September and the first supplementary ques tion to Oral Question No 1 yesterday, does
5882 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Oct 2012
he now know on what date the Government Communications Security Bureau was first
told that its surveillance of Kim Dotcom was illegal?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am advised by the Government
Communications Security Bureau that the fi rst time it became aware its activity in
relation to the Dotcom case was unlawful was between 7 September, when an affidavit
was filed in the court, and 13 September, when my office was informed. As I have
previously stated publicly, ther e were two main aspects to the human error at the heart
of this matter: first, the Government Communi cations Security Bureau originally relied
on the police information about the residency status of the people in question and did
not check further, and, second, the error was compound ed after the operation was
concluded by a simple wrong interpretation of the law, which occurred in February, as I
have stated publicly several times.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Did the Government Communications  Security Bureau mention the
police operation of Kim Dotcom at either or bo th of the briefings that it gave him on 14
and 24 February?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given his answer yesterday, has he now gone and asked his
department, the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, what, if any, knowledge
it had of the Kim Dotcom case prior to September?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: A member of the Department of the Prime Minister and
Cabinet was aware of the Government Comm unications Security Bureau’s involvement
after the raid took place; that would have been in late January. That information was
never passed on to me. We have looked at  all of the records and notes and email
correspondence, and the person has confirmed th at they never discussed the matter with
me, and has actually never discussed the matter with me.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Who was that person who did not pass on that information to him?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Roy Ferguson.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Which of his ministerial colleagues, other than the Attorney-
General, did he discuss the Government Communications S ecurity Bureau’s unlawful
surveillance of Mr Dotcom with prior to the bureau’s actions being made public?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not know the answer to those questions.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: How, then, can he be sure he actually spoke to Ministers if he
cannot actually recall who they were?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I remember having a discussi on; I think it was with the
Attorney-General. I am sure there were anot her couple of Ministers there, but I do not
recall who they were.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Mr Speaker—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I want to hear the—[ Interruption] Order! Order! I say to the
Labour members to show their leader some courtesy. I want to hear his question.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Will he confirm that he had not heard of Kim Dotcom or
Megaupload prior to 19 January?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Correct.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: On the question of the Prim e Minister’s knowledge or
memory, does he stand by his written answer to my ques tion of 7 May when he was
asked what dates between 7 April and 23 Ju ly 2011 he met with the Hon Simon Power
following Mr Power’s seeking further inform ation on Kim Dotcom, and can he assure
the House that Mr Power did not raise the subject of Kim Dotcom at that 13 June 2011
meeting?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I can confirm he did not raise the matter.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How can the Prime Minister make that assurance when in
his written answer to my question on 7 May he claimed: “There is no record of what
17 Oct 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5883
was discussed … and I have no recollection of the discussion.”? How could he give that
assurance to the House today?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As I distinctly recall, the firs t I heard of Kim Dotcom was 19
January 2012.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How can the Prime Minister possibly give an assurance
that that matter was not raised by the Hon Simon Power with  him back in June 2011, as
he just did, when in his formal writing to me in a written answer he said: “There is no
record of what was discussed … and I have  no recollection of the discussion.”? How
can he reconcile those two statements: the one today in the House and the written one?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Quite easily, because I do not recall the exact conversation of
why Simon came to me on that particular occasion, but I know for a fact it was not
about Kim Dotcom.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order,  Mr Speaker. Mr Speaker—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! A point of order has been called.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I seek leave to table this question and answer—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We do not table questions  for written answer. They are
available to all members anyhow.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, a further supplementary question?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member, I think, has used his allocation of supplementary
questions available.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, I seek leave to get the truth out of the Prime
Minister.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member can seek leave only fo r a procedure of the House to be
followed.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The idea that you would
indicate that getting the truth out of the Prime Minister is not a procedure—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume his seat. This is the House of
Representatives. We do not need that sort of nonsense.
Grandparents and Other Kin Carers—Parenting Support
4. ALFRED NGARO (National)  to the Minister for Social Development : What
recent announcements has she made regarding providing extra financial assistance to
grandparents raising grandchildren and other kin-carers?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I have announced
my commitment to provide extra financia l assistance to grandparents raising
grandchildren and other kin carers. Although this group of carers get the same basic
payment as those fostering children in the care of Child, Youth and Family, they do not
receive additional assistance for things like clothing, whic h Child, Youth and Family
caregivers get through the foster care allowance.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: I seek leave for the Social Security (Clothing Allowances for
Orphans and Unsupported Children) Amendment Bill in my name to be introduced and
set down as members’ order of the day No. 1 today.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection?
There is objection.

items.speaker: Alfred Ngaro
items.text: Why do you think grandparents and other kin carers need this extra
financial support?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Grandparents have brought up their own families and are
often now in a period of their lives when they are not financially prepared for the costs
of raising a new family. It is  likely that these children have had a hard time in many
cases and need extra support. We know that these children will have better outcomes if
5884 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Oct 2012
they are raised within a loving and stable environment. I have huge admiration for these
kin carers who take on the significant responsib ility of raising these children often in
need.

items.speaker: Alfred Ngaro
items.text: How will you work with these gr oups to see that they get the
financial support they need?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We will go out to these groups and these people to work
out with them what this will look like. We  need to know from them what is most
important to them. It will not look exactly the same as the assistance that non-kin carers
get. We do not want to undermine or override familial responsibilities. For example, I
think it would be inappropriate to give gr andparents money so that they can buy their
own grandchildren presents, but there are ce rtainly areas where they need and deserve
more support.
Manufacturing Sector—Comparison of 2008 and 2012 Export Statistics
5. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance : When he said
yesterday that with a “relatively high” exchange rate, our exporters “have been
sufficiently resilient to be ab le to grow export volumes and value” did he mean that all
export sectors have been growing, and accord ing to Statistics New Zealand, in 2008
dollars what is the percentage change in e xports of simply and el aborately transformed
manufactured goods from the 2008 to 2012 financial years?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: To the first part of the member’s
question, what I meant was that exporters have been sufficiently resilient to be able to
grow export volumes and value, and, indeed, that is what has been happening. To the
second part of his qu estion, I am advised by Statistics  New Zealand that there is no
existing series that perfectly covers his request. In fact, it does not make a lot of sense to
deflate exports by the Consumers Price Inde x, but a close approximation can be made
from the export volume index for non-food manufactured goods. This series shows
manufacturing exports in constant dollar terms, which is what the member appears to be
after. The series shows that there has been  an increase in manufacturing export volumes
of 3.9 percent between the ye ar to June 2008 and the year  to June 2012, despite the
recession and a global financial crisis.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why is the Minister using volume terms? Is it because, outside
of primary products, in real terms manufactur ing is declining? In  fact, there is a 14
percent decline in simply transformed manufactured exports and a 10 percent decline in
elaborately transformed manufactured exports. Is he not aware of that?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We can have a contest of different statistics if the member
likes. The fact is that the Statistics New Zealand series  of export volume for non-food
manufactured goods shows an increase, even in constant dollar terms. Total exports
have been rising after a bit of a dip from the global financial crisis. The value of exports
has risen 13 percent in the last 2 years. Bo th volumes and prices have risen over that
time. As I have pointed out in the answer to an earlier question, the number of people
employed in manufacturing did drop in the la st 2 years of the previous Government’s
time in office, but, actually, since 2009 it  has fluctuated between 245,000 and 255,000
people. So the member can look as hard as he likes, but it will be difficult for him to
create a sense of crisis for manufacturing.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: If, according to his own Government statistics department, there
has been a 14 percent decline and a 10 percent decline in value in simply and
elaborately transformed manuf acturing exports but he still thinks the sector is doing
well, how much more would exports in these s ectors have to decline in value before he
thought there was a serious problem?
17 Oct 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5885

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There may be categories of ma nufacturing exports that have
declined. That is the nature of the recovery  that we are in. Some businesses are doing
well; some are doing poorly. Some sector s are doing well; some are doing poorly. The
fact is that for manufacturing the measure that means the most, in my view, is the
number of people employed in  it, and the number of people employed in it declined in
the last 2 years of the previous Labour Government. Since 2009 it has fluctuated
between 245,000 and 255,000 people, so there is  not a crisis in manufacturing over job
losses. There is a lot of pressure on exporters, who are trying to be profitable despite the
global financial problems.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given that the International Monetary Fund’s most recent World
Economic Outlook  said that New Zealand’s current account deficit this year will be
second worst after Greece, and in 2013 and 2017 is projected by the IMF to be the worst
in the developed world, how can he sit back and not take seriously  the decline in non-
primary manufacturing and the related job losses?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As has been pretty clear, we dispute the member’s
conclusion. The fact is that the job number s in manufacturing have been remarkably
constant despite the global fi nancial crisis and worldwide r ecession. That is a tribute to
the businesses and their staff, who have show n remarkable resilience and attention to
productivity and profitability, and have ma intained hundreds of thousands of jobs
through one of the worst economic times we have seen in decades.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: With New Zealand’s current account deficit forecast by the
IMF to be the worst in the developed world ne xt year, and with inflation for the year at
0.8 percent below the target range of the Reserve Bank, does he now agree that boosting
exports should be a higher priority than further reductions in inflation?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The effective decisions about the interest rates will actually
be made by the Governor of the Reserve Bank. The Government and the new governor
re-signed a policy targets agreement that is no t substantially different from the one that
was in place before or, in fact, the one that was in place under the previous Labour
Government. It is up to the governor to make  those kinds of decisions about whether he
believes interest rates should be raised or lowered.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Actually, the question was
carefully worded to seek his opinion, asking “does he now agree”, and it was on a
policy matter, not on an operational matter to  do with inflation control, because it
addressed the balance—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I hear the member, but I think the member is experienced
enough to recognise in the Mini ster’s answer that the Mini ster answered all that a
Minister of Finance can. The member knows that under the current New Zealand
legislation it is not a matter for the Minist er of Finance to even express opinions on
those matters. Ministers of Finance need to  be careful about e xpressing opinions on
those matters. They are the responsibility of the Governor of the Reserve Bank.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Given that the policy targets agreement that the Minister has
just referred to sets a midpoi nt target of 2 perc ent inflation per annum, and given that
inflation is now at 0.8 percen t below the bottom end of the target range, may I repeat:
does he believe that promoting exports and the use of policy tool s by his ministry,
Treasury, and not the Reserve Bank, would now take a higher priority in his
Government’s policy programme than achie ving further reductions  of inflation by
compressing the economy further into a rut?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am not quite sure what the last bit means, but the
Government has focused strongly, sinc e taking office, on reinforcing the
competitiveness of our export industries. They  lost a lot of competitiveness through the
first decade of this century. In the light of  the global financial crisis and recession
5886 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Oct 2012
around the world, it is vital that we continue  the programme laid out in a number of
documents that have been published, and some  that will be published, on the Business
Growth Agenda, which is designed to enable  our businesses to more easily make the
decision to invest, to expand, to employ more people, to make prof its, and also to pay
tax, and the Government will stay focused on that.
Child Poverty—Income Tax (Universalisation of In-work Tax Credit) Amendment
Bill
6. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he stand
by his statement, in response to a question about whether he will support my Income
Tax (Universalisation of In-work Tax Credit ) Amendment Bill that “she wants to give
the same millionaires yet more money to raise their kids”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I stand by my full statement, which made
reference to the member’s support in genera l for a universal child payment. That full
statement in relation to children living in difficult circumstances was: “This
Government spends a huge amount of time,  money, and energy focused on those young
New Zealanders and on trying to give them help . If the member thinks that that will be
resolved without giving them a decent educ ation—because she does not support all the
measures that this Government has taken to lift education standards—then she is
dreaming. If the member thinks that that can be achieved by a universal payment, as I
said to the member some time ago, she co mes into this House and she bags the
Government because she argues that we have  people who are well off, and then she
wants to give the same millionaires yet more money to raise their kids.”

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is the Prime Minister aware that my bill is an opportunity to lift
100,000 children out of poverty, but would have no effect at all on millionaires and the
rich, who would remain ineligible for the in-work tax credit, just as they are now?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, broadly I am aware of it, although I am also advised that
if the in-work tax credit equivalent was paid to beneficiary families, it would cost more
than $1.5 billion over 4 years.  I do not know the financial costs of the member’s
payment.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is he aware that one of the key goals of the Working for Families
package when it was established was to lif t incomes “for families with dependent
children … as a means of tackli ng child poverty;”, and does he think that it is fair for
the poorest children in New Zealand to continue to be excluded from that goal?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In answer to the first part of the question, yes, but in terms of
the second part of the question, the member should be aware—or is aware—that, in fact,
benefit-based households receive Working for Families. What they do not receive is the
in-work tax credit.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does he think that it is fair to deny this little bit of extra financial
support to the 36 percent of M āori children who liv e in benefit-reliant households and
who do not get access to the in-work tax credit, even where their parents also work?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I cannot comment on the last bi t, because it is subject to
everybody’s household, depending on whether they  get the in-work tax credit or not,
because if their income is high enough, then it  is abated. But, in principle, the in-work
tax credit when it was designed by a Labour Government was to make sure that there
was always a differential between working a nd welfare. And the re ason for that, and
rightfully so, when Michael Cullen put that scheme together, was that he wanted to
make sure there was an incentive for people to move off benefits into work. He was
right to do that, because quite a lot of research indicates that  the fastest way to lift poor
households that have children in poverty out  of that poverty situation is through work.
In fact, the Children’s Commissioner’s expert group said this: “Research indicates that a
17 Oct 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5887
parent obtaining full-time paid employment is  the most important event to lift children
out of poverty.” If the member wants to lift those children out of poverty, may I suggest
she work and focus on getting their families into work.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is it fair that because M āori joblessness has grown by 80 percent
under his Government, thousands of M āori children have lost access to the in-work tax
credit as a direct consequence of his Government’s economic failures?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I refute the last point. Firstly, this is a Government where
growth has been 1.6 percent for the first half  of this year, where 57,000 jobs have been
created in the last 2 years, and where we are growing faster than most other OECD
countries. Secondly, what is true is that if somebody is in work and then loses their job,
they will lose the in-work tax credit. But I would also hasten to add that if someone then
takes a part-time job, even for 20 hours or more, to the best  of my memory, they then
get the in-work tax credit back. So therefore I think that is a pretty good scheme.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Prime Minister not unde rstand even the existing policy,
which says that whether they work 20 hours or  not, if they also are in receipt of a
benefit or a student allowance or superannuation they are not eligible for the in-work tax
credit, because they receive a means-tested be nefit, and that is the discrimination that
has been found to exist that traps—lock s—100,000 children or more into poverty,
because he does not even understand his own policy?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do, but what the member is arguing is that someone should
get an in-work tax credit when they are on a benefit. What you cannot do is get both.
What currently happens, t hough, is that everybody under a cer tain income level gets
Working for Families.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Prime Minister accept that children are actually going
hungry in this country, and that their parents do not have enough money to feed them or
to accommodate them in warm, dry homes, and will he help thousands of these children
today by supporting a simple, pragmatic bill to  extend the support that is given to other
children to those who need it the very most?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In answer to the last part of the member’s question, no, we
will not be supporting the bill.  In terms of whether ther e are some children in New
Zealand in very poor conditions, the answer to th at is yes, but then I think we also need
to take a step back and say that the Gove rnment does a huge range of things, including
making sure there is universal provision of  welfare support. There is emergency or
hardship support, there is State hous ing provided, there are accommodation
supplements, and there are many other provis ions of support from the Government to
those who are in the worst scenario. I say to the member that this is a Government that
is working hard to address those issues with all sorts of things, from insulation of homes
to trying to get rid of rheumatic fever.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Prime Minister think th at the Children’s Commissioner’s
Expert Advisory Group on Solutions to Child Poverty, the Child Poverty Action Group,
the Every Child Counts coali tion of community organisati ons, and other experts are
wrong to conclude that my b ill would make a real differe nce to the poverty suffered by
thousands of New Zealand children every day? Are they all wrong?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Around 60 percent of kids who are living in poverty are in
benefit-dependent households. That is why, to quote her, the Children’s
Commissioner’s expert group—the very gr oup she just quoted—said, and I quote this
again, “Research indicates that a parent obtaining full-time paid employment is the most
important event to lift children out of poverty.”

Primary Growth Partnership—Successful Bids and Purpose
7. SHANE ARDERN (National—Taranaki - King Country)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Primary Industries
items.text: What progress can he report on  the Primary Growth Partnership
Initiative?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: I have recently
announced the Government is to fund nearly half of a $14.6 million programme, led by
PGG Wrightson Seeds, to develop new pasture and forage crop technology. This
successful bid lifts the total amount of Government and industry funding under the
Primary Growth Partnership to around $600 million. In just 3 years the Primary Growth
Partnership has worked with industry to de velop some of the most exciting primary
sector research and innovation proposals that New Zealand has ever seen.

items.speaker: Shane Ardern
items.text: Why has the Government committed funding to improving
innovation and productivity in the primary sector?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: This Government has set ambitious targets of increasing
exports to 40 percent of GDP and encour aging the business sector to double its
expenditure on research and development to  more than 1 percent of GDP. As the
primary sector makes up 71 percent of New Z ealand’s merchandise exports, it is clear
that this sector will play a crucial part in achieving thes e targets. Increasing innovation
investment in our food, fishing, fibre, and fore stry industries is crucial to the success of
the New Zealand economy.

items.speaker: Shane Ardern
items.text: Has the Primary Growth Partners hip been successful in providing
funding to a wide range of firms?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: Yes, it certainly has. I am very pleased to report that over a
quarter of a billion dollars of Government  funding has been allocated across a wide
range of firms, big and small. The Primary Gr owth Partnership initiative is encouraging
buy-in by industry righ t across a range of business, it is encouraging new, innovative
investment, and it is encour aging industry to work togeth er in order to make New
Zealand a more productive and competitive economy. The Primary Growth Partnership
has been highly successful.
Social Development, Ministry—Reports on Security of Private Information
8. JACINDA ARDERN (Labour)  to the Minister for Social Development : What
vulnerabilities were identified in the report prepared by Dimension Data on the security
of the Work and Income kiosks?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The Dimension Data
report found an issue with th e lack of network separatio n whereby the kiosks were
connected directly to the Ministry of Social Development network, meaning that
sensitive documents were accessible from th e kiosks. This report sparks the obvious
question of whether this issue was addre ssed and the problems fixed, and given the
situation we are now in, it is clear that th ey were not. This is why the chief executive
and I decided to release this information public ly yesterday, in an effort to be upfront
and honest about what we are actually dealing with.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Did she receive any reports, either verbal or written, on
vulnerabilities within the ministry’s systems at the time that that report was prepared?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: What did her monitoring of the roll-out of her new automated
systems involve, given this is what she undertook she would do in 2009?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: That monitoring of those syst ems was more than just the
kiosks, actually. As you can see, we have  got My Account, where people can now
17 Oct 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5889
access their own information online, and we ha ve about 12 percent who actually go into
the kiosks—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: The Minister was looking at their accounts?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Oh, let us not be ridiculous, Trevor Mallard, like you like
to be. So what we have got now is we have got—so that whole question of we are going
more online was about more than just the ki osks; it was about a ra nge of information. I
was advising the Minister that we would be looking at how quickly that is rolled out and
what the cost is, and that is exactly what we have done.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I was very specific in my
question around what the monitoring exactly en tailed. I would have liked the Minister
to address the substantive part of that question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Well, I think the member’s questioning is, in fact, serious, and is
appropriate questioning. I think it should be treated with more respect by the member’s
colleagues. The member’s colleagues sought to  interject and the Mi nister responded to
those interjections. I am not goi ng to now ask the Minister to ignore all of that and give
a precise answer.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Oh, just protecting the weak Ministers.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member knows he cannot do that . I am not sure on what basis
the member, the Hon Trevor Mallard, thinks th at that is appropriate. I am not going to
ask the member to leave. I do not want to gi ve the member that dignity. I just want him
to know how childish I think that is.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Did Dimension Data contact the ministry to correct the chief
executive’s claim that it had not reported on vulnerabilities in the system, or did
someone within the ministry check the report?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I first saw the report on Monday night at about 8 o’clock.
It had been seen that day. It was afte r 1 o’clock, when we had done the press
conference. It was then brought to our attent ion that, without a doubt , it had raised this
particular issue. By quarter past 9 the ne xt morning we had put out a press release
letting everyone know that.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. My question was specifically
who identified that the report had found the vulnerabilities, but that was not reported.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member may repeat her question.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Did Dimension Data contact the ministry to correct the chief
executive’s claim that it had not reported on vulnerabilities in the system, or did
someone within the ministry go back and check the report?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: As far as I know there was not a phone call from
Dimension Data, but I do not know that. There may have been. But, as I say, it was first
brought to my attention that night, and as a consequence we put the press release out the
next morning.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Is public confidence in her mi nistry’s management of sensitive
data an operational issue?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I think the confidence of this is everyone’s issue, and it is
one that I am taking very, very seriously. It has been undermined. I think it is appalling
that this information has been accessed. I have done everything I can, since knowing
this on Sunday evening, to make sure that we get to the bottom of it, we fix it, and we
make sure it never ever happens again.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: When the Minister said yesterday concerning the Work and Income

items.speaker: New Zealand kiosk security breach
items.text: “I ha ve not leaked private information about
individuals.”, does she deny that in July 2009 she instructed her staff to release the
benefit details of two women on the DPB, without their permission, prompting a Human
5890 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Oct 2012
Rights Commission investigation into her ac tions and the Direct or of Human Rights
Proceedings finding that she had deliberately breached these women’s privacy?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have some difficulty with this  supplementary question, because it
bears no relationship whatsoever to the vul nerabilities identified in the report by
Dimension Data. I am thinking back on the Mi nister’s answers today, and the Minister
has not mentioned any of those issues in her answers. I do not want to deprive the
member of her supplementary question. I invite the member to ask another
supplementary question that really relates to the primary question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: How can it be anything but a clear failure of her leadership, when she
has legitimised the breach of privacy by her ministry by having previously done so
herself, without remorse, and when she has failed to demonstrate any oversight of
ongoing breaches of privacy by not ensuring th at her ministry fixed major security
problems brought to its attention not once, not twice, but now three times in 2 years?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I have not leaked any information or any beneficiaries’
information. That member may struggle with that, but I transparently put it out there
and did it myself without any private comm ent. I know that the Opposition struggles
with that, because those members prefer to  pass little notes under doorways to the
media, and everything else. I point-blankly went out there and said what I said. So there
has been no leak from me.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Given the Minister’s assurances to  the public that she was mortified
by the breach by the ministry and that she was looking for the utmost transparency in
dealing with the issue, how can she expect New Zealanders to have any confidence at

question her policy, without their consent, can be trusted to oversee any kind of privacy
management in the ministry?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We have a serious system flaw that this Government has
taken very seriously. We have taken action— the best and the quickest that we possibly
can. We will not undermine it. Actually, that member is not the only one who gets to
wring their hands and do angst. We are very  concerned on this si de and are taking it
very seriously.
Surgical Services—Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Programme
9. Dr JACKIE BLUE (National)  to the Minister of Health : What reports has he
received on improving the quality and efficiency of health services?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Under the Government, public hospitals
are making smarter use of their resources to treat more patients and get these patients
home to their families sooner. Part of this is the new Enhanced Recovery After Surgery
programme, which helps people recover more quickly and safely after their operation,
so they can have fewer complications and get home to their families sooner. This is now
being used in South Auckland, the Bay of Plenty, Wellington, Nelson, Marlborough,
Southern, and Waitematā, and is expected to be rolled out to other district health boards
over time.

items.speaker: Dr Jackie Blue
items.text: How does the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery programme help
to get patients home sooner?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Under the programme, patients are given a comprehensive
early preoperative assessment, where they are encouraged to get their bodies as fit as
possible in preparation for surgery and anaes thesia. Then the surgical techniques used
are less invasive and with di fferent types of anaesthesia. For example, prior to this
programme a patient receiving bowel surgery would take several days before they could
get out of bed, and many more days before they could return home. With this new
programme our clinicians are now able to see that these patients are able to eat and
17 Oct 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5891
drink and are out of bed on the day of surger y, and walking the ward on the very next
day. This means that these people are hom e with their families sooner, and I think
everyone would join with me in congratulat ing our clinicians on their leader ship in
changing their approaches to surgery to provide this better service.

items.text: Is she confident that the assessment of damage at each of the schools

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: As I acknowledged in my answer to the primary question,

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Will the schools proposed for merger or closure be given extra time
to consult with their communities, given that they were given the ministry’s estimate of

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: From the time the proposals were launched on 13

makes it clear that there are different phase s available for this consultation through to

to listen to the views of parents and the school communities, and I will take, along with
them, the time that it will take. We—all of us—a re interested in getting this right and
getting in place the best possible education system for the Greater Christchurch region.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I am not entirely sure the

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I think Ministers are at li berty to answer—in my view, that

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. What I said was—

items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. With respect, you

Canterbury, Recovery—Insurance Cover
12. CHRIS AUCHINVOLE (National)  to the Minister for Canterbury

items.speaker: Earthquake Recovery
items.text: What reports has he received on the availability of insurance
cover to support the rebuilding of Canterbury following the seismic events?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I
am pleased to report that in addition to th e maintenance of existing insurance cover for
Cantabrians, new insurance cover packag es are now offered by Westpac, BNZ,
Kiwibank, ANZ, ASB, and existing insurance companies. There are now a range of
5896 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Oct 2012
providers competing to cover existing, an d the construction of  new, residential
properties. Contract works cover for the c onstruction of new commercial facilities is
available, with brokers actively touting for that business. Insurance risk will not be
transferred, therefore, to the taxpayers, and that means that the ongoing risk continues to
lie on international balance sheets.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: Has the Crown been asked to take over insurance cover provision
in Christchurch?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: There were a number of calls from Opposition
members to take on insurance risk for what will be a multibillion-dollar rebuild of
Christchurch. But as professional risk asse ssors monitor Canterbury they are noting the
GNS Science predictions of reduced seismic risk. With that information, they are
increasingly willing to increase the level of insurance available in the region, which
means that insurance risk need not be tr ansferred to the Crown beyond the Earthquake
Commission and Southern Response—former AMI—exposures.
Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment
Bill—Commentary
1. ANDREW WILLIAMS (NZ First)  to the Member in charge of the Reserve
Bank of New Zealand (Ame nding Primary Function of Bank) Amendment Bill : Is
the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Amendi ng Primary Function of Bank) Amendment
Bill a “snake oil solution that would achieve nothing”?
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Member in ch arge of the Reserve Bank of New
Zealand (Amending Primary Functi on of Bank) Amendment Bill) : It is
demonstrably nothing of the sort. It is a vita l and urgently needed bill. The bill will
enable the Reserve Bank to take positive ac tion to lower the value of the New Zealand
dollar and bring relief to the hard-pressed expo rt sector, most of whom are in National
Party electorates. We are in a new econom ic era and need a Reserve Bank Act that
reflects the new realities.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: What are businesses and, in pa rticular, broking houses saying
about the Reserve Bank of New Zeala nd (Amending Primary Function of Bank)
Amendment Bill?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: There is wide support from the business and export
sectors for the bill. For example, accordi ng to Bernard Doyle of Australian broking
house JBWere, the Reserve Bank’s current orthodox monetary policy is becoming “a
rarity in the global economy” and “Unfortuna tely, in a world where the major central
banks are breaking all the rules, this is not an advantage.”
Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment
Bill—Proposed Changes to Bank’s Function
2. ANDREW WILLIAMS (NZ First)  to the Member in charge of the Reserve
Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primar y Function of Bank) Amendment Bill :
What are the flaws in the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989 that the Reserve
Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment Bill seeks to
address?
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Member in ch arge of the Reserve Bank of New
Zealand (Amending Primary Func tion of Bank) Amendment Bill) : Another
superbly drafted question. The current Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act puts
unwarranted emphasis on price stability, and does not allow the Reserve Bank to pursue
a broad mandate for economic policy that covers growth, exports, and jobs. The original
Act, of course, was to try to combat the dogs of inflation unleashed by the neo-liberals
17 Oct 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5897
in this country—much subscribed to by the present administration. The focus on
inflation in the current Act, to the neglect of other important economic indicators—

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Us neo-liberals hate being attacked like that.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: —and Maurice Williamson has learnt nothing as
well in all that time—has lead to a chr onically overvalued exchange rate, which is
seriously undermining New Zealand’s international competitiveness.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: Why is it necessary to broaden the primary functions of the
Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989 as this bill proposes?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: The reason is that the current Reserve Bank is no
longer fit for purpose in the current econom ic era. The general consensus among
economic commentators is that in the wa ke of the global financial crisis the
international economy faces a prolonged peri od of sluggish growth and increased
volatility. All manner of senior economists and the IMF say the same. What we do
know is that our current Re serve Bank of New Zealand Act is now seriously out of
kilter with the prevailing international economic conditions—in particular, low
inflation, along with the intense efforts by many countries  to hold the value of their
currencies down. The West Coast and Rodney would love to have this, as well.
Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment
Bill—Proposed Changes to Principal Act
3. ANDREW WILLIAMS (NZ First)  to the Member in charge of the Reserve
Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primar y Function of Bank) Amendment Bill :
What other functions will the Reserve Bank of New Zeala nd (Amending Primary
Function of Bank) Amendment Bill seek to include in section 8 of the principal Act?
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Member in ch arge of the Reserve Bank of New
Zealand (Amending Primary Functi on of Bank) Amendment Bill) : The Reserve
Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment Bill will
allow the bank to incorporate into its monetary policy the goal of achieving a stable and
competitive exchange rate, an d all over provincial New Ze aland they cannot wait for
this bill to pass. The bill will enable the appropriate authority and importance to be
attached to economic growth and employme nt, as well as the desperately needed
promotion of exports in an export-dependent nation.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: What would the latest CPI figur es mean for the Reserve Bank if
the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Amendi ng Primary Function of Bank) Amendment
Bill became law?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: That is a very apposite question. If the Reserve Bank
of New Zealand (Amending Primary Functi on of Bank) Amendment Bill was treated
seriously by serious legislators, and not jeered at because of neo-liberal antagonism, and
became law, it would mean that the bank could take a full account of prevailing
economic conditions—that is, that inflation no longer needs to be the primary target and
the only imperative of economic policy. The Reserve Bank would, as an example, be
better able to take into account the latest CPI figures in formulating a rational monetary
policy that met New Zealand’s broader econom ic policy objectives. If a man as bright
as Lee Kuan Yew could see the sense in this, I wonder why those members cannot.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I move, That the House take
note of miscellaneous business . This is a Government in to tal disarray. There has never
been a time in New Zealand’s political hi story when so many Government agencies
have been out of control, a nd without leadership. The Minist ry of Social Development,
5898 General Debate 17 Oct 2012
the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Tr ade, and the Government Communications
Security Bureau are the examples just this week, and it starts at the top.
It starts at the top with the Prime Mini ster—the Prime Minister who says “I don’t
know.”, “I can’t remember.”, “I’m not in a position to comment on that.”, and “Who
knows? I crack jokes from time to time. I cr ack jokes about all kinds of important
material.” Well, the message for John Key is  this: New Zealanders want hope; they do
not want Bob Hope. And that is what they are getting from this Prime Minister—he is
cracking the jokes but not doing the job that New Zealanders expect of him.
His Government is in disa rray, and it starts at th e top of the Government
Communications Security Burea u. We entrust in the Prime Minister, as the Minister
who is in control of the Government  Communications Security Bureau, the
responsibility on behalf of al l of us to look after the s py agencies, to look after our
security, and yet this Minister—John Key—ha s no idea what is ha ppening in his own
agency. He has not been briefed. He does not  know what is happening. That is the story
he is asking New Zealanders to believe.
That is the story he want s New Zealanders to believe , but day by day his story
unravels. Day by day he has to admit that he got it wrong. He said “It was not
September; it was really February.” and “I am not going to be  talking about Kim
Dotcom in Hollywood. Oh, no, I am going to be talking about Kim Dotcom in
Hollywood.” Mr Key’s story is unravelling da y by day, and his lack of leadership, his
lack of focus on these agencies, is going to come to this House again, and we will see it.
But it goes right across the National Party front bench. If the National Party had a
Malcolm Tucker from The Thick of It , he would have a desk placed in Hekia Parata’s
office. It would be there permanently as he tried to unravel what it is that she is telling
this House. But what we know on this side of the House is that she has treated the
people of Christchurch shabbily. That is  what she has done. She has not gone down
there and looked at these problems. She has not even got a proper assessment of each
school. She has simply gone there with a one-size-fits-all so lution, and that is
disrespectful to the people of Christchurch. Her story unravels every day as well.
Then there is Paula Bennett and the Ministry  of Social Development. The ministry
was told about the weaknesses and vulnerabilities in its system, and it did nothing. It did
absolutely nothing. In 2009 Paula Bennett to ld John Key that sh e would be closely
monitoring everything that went on, and sh e completely failed to do that. She is
overseeing an agency that is in disarray. We have had that, we have had ACC—this
Government is letting New Zealanders down.
New Zealanders have a right to be disa ppointed in this Government, because John
Key came into office and told New Zealande rs: “I expect high standards from my
Ministers.” That is what he told New Zeala nders. Well, he, today, in his ministry, has a
Minister in John Banks who has consisten tly misled New Zealanders and who has
consistently misled the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister clings on to the political
corpse that is John Banks to save his Govern ment’s majority. Well, what he is doing is
letting down the standards of  ministerial behaviour and letting down New Zealanders.
He is not upholding the standards he sa id he would, and he  is not upholding the
standards that New Zealanders would expect. He is now seen in the eyes of many New
Zealanders as being the one th ing that John Key always fear ed: just anothe r politician.
But he is worse than that. He has lowered the standards of mini sterial accountability,
and New Zealanders have every right to be disappointed in him.
The other thing that this Government is  doing is overseeing a decline in the New
Zealand economy. It is not even prepared to take its head out of the sand, to stop
practising the ostrich economics that this Government seems to think are OK, to
actually look at the loss of jobs around New Zealand and say to New Zealanders “We
17 Oct 2012 General Debate 5899
will be there with you.” Instead, it is prepar ed to sit on the sidelines of the economy,
waiting for something to happen. Instead of  doing what any good Government would
do, which is to get in there, get its hands dirty, and help New Zealanders create jobs, the
Government waits, and it sits on the sidelin es. This is a Government in disarray,
managing a decline. New Zealand can do better.  Labour will have a better path for New
Zealand than this.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I wonder whether Grant

items.speaker: Robertson asked David Shearer
items.text: “Where’s the tape?”.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think he did. I wonder whet her he asked him in caucus:
“Where’s the tape?”. I wonder why he aske d the questions he did yesterday in the
House designed to make David Shearer l ook stupid over the tape. There is one thing
that has become very clear from watchi ng those Opposition members, for that very
small number of New Zealanders who bother doing it, which is that they are much more
ambitious for themselves than they are for New Zealanders. There is absolutely no
doubt about that, because this lazy, trite O pposition has almost nothing to contribute to
the real debates. I am sure those member s will debate for the next week, or month
perhaps, among themselves whether the na me of some guy who found the problem in
the Work and Income computer was leaked or not leaked, because that is the stuff they
like. That is the stuff they like. Was it l eaked? Did Grant say to David, the right way
round: “I support you.”?
Actually the big questions are being addressed by the Greens and New Zealand
First. Should we be printing money? Well, the answer is no. S hould we throw out the
Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act? Well, the answer is no, we should not. But at least
they are putting up something substantial that is relevant to the concerns of every New
Zealander—that is, th eir economic security. David Shearer is totally focused on the
security cameras in a building most New Zealanders have never seen.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: He’s more focused on it than J ohn Key is, and he’s meant to be
the Minister.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, he was put there as Leader of the Opposition to be like
John Key, and I just want to say this: David Shearer is no John Key, and I think
everybody knows that. Everybody knows that.
The Prime Minister is leading a Governme nt that is relentlessly focused on the
economy, and the performance of the New Zealand economy, by international
standards, has been very good. I was going to say pretty good, but as more other
developed economies trend towards re cession, the New Zealand economy is
maintaining 2 to 3 percent growth. That is  providing higher afte r-tax incomes for New
Zealand families. It has provi ded more opportunities for New Zealanders to get jobs. It
has provided the opportunity to maintain  and improve public services under the
leadership of the outstanding Ministers that were attacked today by the Opposition. That
is in sharp contrast to what is happeni ng in virtually every developed economy around
the world—including, I might say, Aust ralia, where large-scale public sector
redundancies, falling house prices, and gr owing unemployment are now what is
happening in the economy that has in recent y ears served us so well as an engine of
growth.
We will stay relentlessly focused on econom ic opportunity and on creating jobs. The
Government has published three or four documents so far, with several to come, which
outline in great detail the numerous ways in  which we are attending to the one decision
that makes a difference to economic growt h, and that is the decision made in a
workplace by a business, its management, and staff, to grow. Until they decide to
employ another person, there is not another job. So we owe a de bt of thanks to all those
5900 General Debate 17 Oct 2012
businesses and workplaces, which through the most difficult economic times in a
generation have continued to grow, and have continued to pay the wages, and to provide
a living for families. That has made it easier for the Government to continue its
programme of support for businesses, thr ough the largest research and development
investment that New Zealand has ever ha d; for families, through the most income
support New Zealand has ever delivered to fa milies; and for public services, which, at
the same time as going through tough times a nd radical change, are offering the highest
level of services and satisfaction that New Zealanders have ever expressed.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: So Mr Shearer is no John Key?
Well, maybe Bill English is right, because I do not know Mr Shearer to be full of
bulldust, I do not understand him to be racked with amnesia, and I do not understand
him to be a “spray and walk away” merchant.
Who knew about Kim Dotcom? Well, that ma n who just sat down did, Bill English,
and he sought to not disclose a public disc losure matter. The Hon Jonathan Coleman,
the then Minister of Immigration, got Dotcom here in the first place. The Hon Maurice
Williamson, the Minister for Land Informati on, approved the Chrisco deal of sale to
Kim Dotcom. Simon Power, the then Associat e Minister of Finan ce and Minister of
Justice, declined Dotcom’s purchase of the Chrisco mansion, and got Williamson to do
a U-turn.
Who else knew? John Banks knew—well, he did know back then. The New Zealand
Police, the Organised and Financial Crim e Agency of New Zealand, and hundreds of
others all knew about Dotcom. And we ha ve seen the backtrac king from the Prime
Minister. First he said  he was told about Do tcom the night before  the raid. That was
demonstrably false. He knew in February this year about the Government
Communications Security Bureau involvement  in the Dotcom case. We know that he
was briefed by the bureau in February on th ree separate occasions. But things are
heating up. The information we are getting in is getting us closer and closer to the Prime
Minister.
In April 2011 Simon Power was in a bit of a pickle about Dotcom’s Overseas
Investment Office application. Although his colleague Maurice Williamson had rubber-
stamped the document, as Maurice always does, Power was not so sure. He wanted
further advice, and on 18 July Power declined Dotcom’s application and phoned the
Prime Minister to tell him—except that the Prime Minister has no recollection. Why
would Power call the Prime Minist er’s office to relay that information to him, if it did
not get to him? More importantly, what  happened on 17 April 2011 and 18 July 2011?
Well, we have found out, from a written question, that on 13 June 2011 Simon Power
met the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister claimed in his reply to that written
question—in his answer, that  is—“no record, no recollection”. Yet today, when asked
“can he assure the House that Mr Power did not  raise the subject of Kim Dotcom at that
13 June 2011 meeting?”, he said yes. One of  those answers is palpably, demonstrably
false.
Is this man’s memory improving with age?  He could not remember about the June
2011 meeting and answer, and today leapt to his feet to give an assurance. Frankly, that
will not do. He is caught out again. We have already got two apologies from him, and
here will come the third one . I hope that this time we ar e not delayed weeks and weeks
and weeks on the most demonstrable, apparent  deceit, and, in my view, a breach of the
privileges of this House and a contempt of Parliament—all in one.
His answer today cannot be correct. He sa id that there was no such conversation
between Mr Power and himself. But he could not remember when he, on record, read it
out in the House. He cannot remember the Tranz Rail shares. He cannot remember the
winery that he did not have  a stake in. He cannot remember the BMWs that he was
17 Oct 2012 General Debate 5901
involved in. “Don’t know, can’t remember”—these are the words that will be the legacy
of this Prime Minister, and they will come back to haunt him, because the good news is,
Mr Brownlee, that there is lots more to come. If the Government even dreamt that this is
going to go away, if it even dreamt that the issue is going to go away, it should wake up
and apologise now.
Well, that last speech by Winston Peters r eally did read like the opening chapter in a

items.speaker: Jeffrey Archer novel
items.text: complete fiction ba sed upon the member’s own loose grasp of
facts, in his own case, throughout his own political career. There is no one in this House
who is more condemned by amnesia than that member over there.
We have had a very interesting week so far in Parliament. Last week we saw the
Opposition parties’ David Shearer, Winston Peters, and Russel Norman cosy up on a
bench—oh, I am sorry, David Shearer and Ru ssel Norman were cosying up; Winston
Peters was an arm’s length away—showing th e nation what an alternative coalition
might look like and claiming that there is a job crisis in this country. So having gone out
there and spruiked all this up, what did they do when th ey came into the House this
week? They went back on to the old stuff of Mr Dotcom, the Government
Communications Security Burea u, and everything else that is completely irrelevant to
the daily lives of New Zealanders.
I have got to say that this side of the H ouse is delighted to look at the question sheet
every day and see that the Labour Party, the New Zealand First Party, and the Green
Party have once again failed New Zealanders by choosing to look at  all of the beltway
stuff that makes very little difference to  New Zealanders’ lives. We had Mr Grant
Robertson come into the House today, and in  his speech in his contribution to this
debate, first up, was he talking about jobs? Was he talking about the difficulties that
people have in their daily lives? No, he was talking about  the Government
Communications Security Bureau and saying what a terrible situation has developed
around it. This is the first member of Parlia ment I have ever seen  stand up and take a
point of order asking the Speaker to stop the member giving the answer from giving the
answer because the answer did not suit his narrative. That was what we got from him
yesterday—completely irrelevant—and now, today, another attempt to try to push along
this Jeffrey Archer - type novel that these guys are collectively writing.
I heard Mr Robertson also say that the Mi nister of Education has failed people in
Christchurch with the education plan. That  is typical of the Labour Party. There are
9,500 spare spaces in schools in Christchurch, there are 4,500 students off the rolls in
Christchurch, and the Labour Party says: “Do not hing. Just leave it all. Just put up with
it.”—just have shonky facilities for these ch ildren in their learni ng opportunities going
forward, and ignore what is a very, very bi g challenge. I am sorry if some of the
members and their mates feel that that does not represent them, but that is what Mr
Robertson had to say in the House today.
What I can say is that in Christchurch, ye s, there is disappointment about this and,
yes, there is disappointment that there were ever the earthquake events in the first place.
But there is also a deep real ism about the need to make good decisions so that we get a
solid recovery, and our young people and our children’s learning are central to that.
I go back to that job summit those members had last week, trying to create the idea
that there is a crisis . The media, sadly, always want to cover a story about some job
losses somewhere, but just look at the record. Since this Government came to office—in
fact, just in the last 2 years—60,000 more New Zealanders have found jobs in New
Zealand. There are 60,000 more jobs net in th e workforce than there were 2 years ago.
There have been 13,000 jobs created through the 90-day tria l. Labour said no to that,
but it created 13,000 new jobs. There are 1,000  new jobs on the Waterview Connection
5902 General Debate 17 Oct 2012
motorway, which is part of a whole progr amme of roads of na tional significance
creating jobs throughout the country. Labour is saying no to that, as well.
There are 350 jobs in the expansion of th e Marsden Point refinery, which is a big
infrastructure project. We can look forward to that being replicated in other parts of the
country through different projects. There are 400 jobs at the IBM centre at Unitec, 500
construction jobs at the Methanex plant in  Taranaki, and 1,500 jobs at Fonterra’s new
dairy plant at Darfield in Canterbury. These are real jobs for New Zealanders who need
them, real opportunities for New Zealanders  who need them, and they occur only
because we have a growing economy.
New Zealanders look every night at the ne ws and they see what is happening around
the rest of the world.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: At a time when 160,000 people have gone to
Australia, when youth unemployment is approa ching 20 percent, and when we have got
the second-highest current account deficit in the world after Greece—and next year it is
projected by the IMF to be the worst in  the world—we have got the Government
members saying that they are managing the economy well. Well, I have got news for
them: they are not, and I know why. It is b ecause they are beset with scandal after
scandal. Their own problems are diverting them from the job of looking after New
Zealanders through proper government. We have got non-primary manufacturing in
decline, and the Government denies there is  a problem there. We have got job losses
from the north to the south, and the Government denies they are there. Mr Brownlee just
quoted job statistics that in clude every job of an hour long. Those statistics are a
complete misrepresentation of what is happening in New Zealand.
What are the scandals? Well, of course, the most recent one is Kim Dotcom. At the
start of the year it was the teapot tapes. Does anyone remember that? John Key and John
Banks getting caught out at a public meeting, being recorded, complaining to the police,
using the police against the media in the el ection, and then miraculously dropping that
because it was going to be embarrassing for the Prime Minister and John Banks to stand
up in court. Then we had the ACC. We had the Bronwyn Pullar affair, followed by the
resignation of the Minister for ACC and the forced resignation of the chair and the
board. Then we had the Budget. In this year ’s Budget, the centrepiece was to improve
student outcomes with larger class sizes. Does anyone reme mber that? There have been
so many scandals since that that one almost  fades into obscurity. What a clanger. Now
we have got the Ministry of Social Deve lopment. In the middle of it we had John
Banks, who asked for donations, received envelo pes with donations in them, made sure
they were banked in Queenstown, thanked the people who gave them, and then signed a
declaration that the donations were anonymous. We know what  a farce that is, and we
have got the Prime Minister trying to pretend that that was in order.
In terms of the economy, what is happening ? Well, we had mining in national parks,
and now the centrepiece for this 3-year triennium is the sale of State-owned assets. We
had “shares plus” off on Monday;  now we have got some sh ares reserved for iwi on
17 Oct 2012 General Debate 5903
Wednesday. What a shambles. No wonder th e economy is not doing what it should. In
terms of Mr Dotcom and the Government Communications Security Bureau and Mr
Key’s role, well what did he say? He said  he did not know anything about it until 17
September. These are all facts that are now proven. Then he said he was briefed on them
on 29 February but could not remember, but ac cepts that he was. Then Labour sources
revealed via David Shearer that on the sa me day, John Key spoke to the staff in the
cafeteria. What did John Ke y do initially? He denied it, and then under further
questioning from Patrick Gower he said th at he remembers that he did—recovered
memory.
We had sources claiming that he had spoke n to people in the cafeteria. Again, John
Key initially denied it and now he says he cannot rule it out. Now he actually admits it
happens. Then we said there was a camera there, and they denied it. Now they admit
they hunted for a camera and they found a camera on a tripod. Now they admit they
have got print photos that were taken—singl e-shot photos. All of this was previously
denied by John Key and somehow  the National Party says th at reflects poorly on David
Shearer. What a nonsense! There is only one person that reflects poorly on, and that is
John Key. Duncan Garner asked whether there was a camera on a tripod, and then
finally the Prime Minister admits that there was. We have got the other allegations made
by Winston Peters today that have not been properly answered.
Scandal after scandal, all year long, and in the meantim e we have got Bill English
not even understanding his ow n statistics that outside of  primary manufacturing we do
have a serious decline in the face of the wo rld’s worst current account deficit. How will
we plug that big hole in New Zealand’s account? There was a $10 billion loss in our
current account last year. It is projected to  get worse—second only to Greece this year
and worst in the world ne xt year. Job losses—160,000 peopl e off to Australia. The
Deputy Prime Minister stood up and said “Oh, it’s going to get better.” Well, it will,
eventually, after 160,000 people have left. That  is more than the total population of
Dunedin and Invercargill combined, and 40 per cent of them are betw een the ages of 18
and 30. Of course, eventually, there will not be that many people left to leave. This
Government is in a shambles and our economy is suffering.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.role: Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector
items.text: It
would seem to me that all the Oppositi on members are worried about—and I disagree
with the Hon Gerry Brownlee; I do not think it is Jeffrey Archer; I think it is the
forensic novels they are into at the mo ment—is what is hidden where. They have
forgotten where the tape is, but they are worried about who said what to whom, and
when. So it is Tess Gerritsen, Kathy Reichs, or Patricia Cornwell they have been
reading, instead of going out and asking New Zealanders: “What matters to you, New
Zealanders?”.
I can answer that question for Opposition members. If you want to know what
matters to New Zealanders, it is their take-home pay, it is their mortgage rate, it is their
interest rates, and it is whether they have got a job. But guess what? This Government is
concentrating on that, not on what was leaked  to whom or what is happening on what
day or the next. New Zealanders want to know that this Government has a programme
of action, and it is about growing the ec onomy. Because, guess what? Governments do
not create jobs. Governments create the enviro nment for jobs to happen in, and that is
what this Government is doing.
Our plan is to deliver a more co mpetitive and productive economy, a robust
economy, which means more jobs for New Zeal anders—real jobs that are sustainable.
Already the Hon Gerry Brownl ee has listed a whole lot of  new jobs, and in my own
patch of Rangitata we had an announcement just  in this last week of 75 to 80 new jobs.
5904 General Debate 17 Oct 2012
Salmon processing is happening here in New Zealand, instead of overseas. You will not
hear anyone in my electorate saying that that is not a good deal.
What other good deals have we got going on here? In the last month 5,230 people
left a benefit. But that is not what Opposition members woul d have happen. They
certainly do not want to see that. We have got GDP figures for the June quarter at 0.6
percent and annual growth of 2.6 percent. It is  the same as Australia, and better than
most. But we do not hear the Opposition cele brating that either, do we? What we have
got at the moment is the lowest inflati on rate since 1999. Does anyone hear Opposition
members talking about that?
Interest rates are at their lowest for 45 years. What does that mean to New
Zealanders? New Zealanders care about those interest rates, because if an individual has
a mortgage of $200,000, what that means is $200 a week more in their pocket. That
does matter to New Zealanders, and the Opposition could not give a—whatever.
We have heard about lots of new jobs, but the problem that we have to face at the
moment is that every time the Government  talks about how to create the environment
for new jobs, Opposition members say “No, we  don’t want you to do that.” They have
totally, all the time, opposed everything we ha ve tried to do, such as reform of the
Resource Management Act, and the 90-day trial, which has created a whole lot of new
jobs for New Zealanders.
The additional programmes of action we put in place over the recession period have
kept people getting something on their CV , like Job Ops and Community Max. They
have kept those people occupied, and have b een very, very successful during that time.
There are many, many companies that are going  to be taking on New Zealanders, such
as Xero, and Orion Health. The International Convention Centre, when it is being built,
will employ heaps of new people. Woolworths , and Heinz Australia are coming back to
New Zealand. There are new jobs here in New Zealand. We have got jobs happening all
over the place.
But Labour members do not want intensification and development of agriculture—of
course not. They do not want more irriga tion, because that might actually mean more
jobs. Labour members would prefer to see people kept on benefits. Just remember, right
now, what are they talking about? They ar e definitely not talking about vulnerable
children, are they? No, they are not. They do not want public sector reform. Actually,
