INCOME TAX (UNIVERSALISATION OF IN-WORK TAX CREDIT)
First Reading

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. T ēnā koutou
katoa e te Whare. I move, That the Income Tax (Universalisation of In-work Tax Credit)
Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Social Services Committee—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Sorry, Metiria. I am just not
sure that I heard that you nominate the Social Services Committee to consider the bill.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: I was just about to.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: My apologies.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: No problem. I nominate the Social Services Committee to
consider this bill. All New Zealand childre n deserve a good life and a fair future. New
Zealand can be, and should be, a great place for our kids to grow  up. But we cannot
deny that for many thousands of children it is  not great. It is a cold and hungry place to
grow up. It is easy for us to  turn away, to blame the pare nts, to blame the economy, to
blame earthquakes or Europe or acts of God, but  it is impossible to deny the facts—the
facts of poverty in our own country—or to deny that we have th e solutions in our
collective hands.
The Children’s Commissioner says that 270,000 New Zealand children live in
poverty. That is more than a quarter of a million New Zealand children. Fifty percent of
these children are M āori or Pacific, and more than  150,000 are reliant on families who
rely on a benefit. These facts are why we s ee on television screen s day after day empty
lunch boxes in school-bags; teachers desperatel y seeking funding to help give their kids
breakfast; increasing illness, hardship, and depr ivation of our littlest citizens; and even
17 Oct 2012 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 5957
reports of kids looking through pig bins fo r food. These are children whom we know.
They go to the same schools as our kids, they play in the same playgrounds as our kids.
They have the same dreams and aspirations, but they do not have the essentials, and
therefore they do not have the opportunities that many of our kids have had.
We could wait for a miraculous growth to  provide thousands of new jobs—and that
is certainly what John Key crosses his fingers for. We  could wait for some new
economic boom to bounce our economy back into the black. But we are not the ones
who are waiting. It is the 150,000 poor kids who are waitin g and paying the price for
this ongoing delay. It is a price that is paid in empty tummies, cold feet, and poor
learning. How can we possibly justify leav ing 150,000 beneficiary kids in poverty? We
simply cannot justify it on any grounds. Such a huge disparity can never be justified in a
country that prides itself on fairness and opportunity.
The solutions to this povert y suffered by kids every day in this country are in our
hands, and we can, if we choose to, give them a fair future. So here is my first step
towards that fair future for our kids. My bill that we are debating tonight will relieve the
worst poverty for these 150,000 children. My bill transforms the in-work tax credit into
a genuine targeted child payment available to all low-income families. It is a step
towards a universal child payment supported by so many in our community.
My bill removes the requirement that a person must work a minimum number of
hours from the current criteria for this tax cr edit. It also removes the restriction that a
person must not be in receipt of a means-te sted benefit, whether that is a welfare
benefit, a student allowance, or supera nnuation—and we know that many grandparents
on superannuation take care of their grandchildren. So this extends the eligibility for the
payment to all low-income families. The bill does not alter the means-test aspect of the
payment, so John Key’s supposed millionaires will not get the payment from this bill,
no matter what he says.
The in-work tax credit was designed to provi de an incentive for people in paid work
and to alleviate child poverty. But it is not delivered as an  incentive. It is actually
delivered as a child payment to alleviate child poverty. The tax cr edit is paid on the
basis of the number of children in the family, and it is paid to the carer of the children,
not to the income earner. It is not related to the cost of work nor to  the hours worked. It
is, in effect, a child payment, and it has been operating well for low-income working
families.
People should be encouraged to work, and increasing the minimum wage and making
the first $10,000 of income tax-free are just a couple of ways to make work really pay.
If this Government is serious about creati ng an incentive for families and for work, it
should not pay that incentive by denying to the poorest kids in this country a child
payment that will help alleviate the worst poverty.
My bill will cost the Government money, and so it should. It w ill cost between $300
and $400 million a year. But compared to the estimated $6 billion a year—the cost of
keeping kids in poverty—it is a very good and very small investment to make in our
littlest citizens. And we do need to make it now, because our kids deserve it. The bill
has been described as a practical and just way to address child poverty, by Auckland
University economics professor, Susan St John. She says that excluding the poorest kids
from the payment as they are now cannot be justified on moral or ethical grounds.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: You rely on Susan St John—far out!

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: It is disturbing that the National members of this House are
barraging from behind me given the serious issue of child poverty that we are facing
today. I think it shows their a ttitude to the issues of poor children who go hungry every
day in this country. In fact , the High Court has held that  the in-work tax credit is
discriminatory in part, and the Child Pove rty Action Group is preparing a case for the
5958 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 17 Oct 2012
Court of Appeal, seeking a ruling that the in-work tax credit discriminates against the
poorest children. I sincerely hope that they succeed to get justice for our kids.
Some from the Government would have you  believe that the poor in New Zealand
are bad parents by definition and deserve nothing more. Bu t through this bill I would
unashamedly put at least $60 extra each week into the back pockets of families who
desperately need it to house, clothe, and feed their kids.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: It’s called communism.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Did you hear that comment from the National member that
feeding kids is communism? I refuse to condemn ordinary New Zealand mums and dads
who are without work. I was one of those mums  once, as were many in this House and
thousands of those in our communities. We  know how tough it can  be, and we only
shame ourselves when we judge others or kick the ladder out fr om behind us, as we
know some have done.
Over the past month, like many New Zeala nders, I have been appalled by the Prime
Minister’s scorn for the seriousness of ch ild poverty, by his refusal to entertain any
solution for these 150,000 childre n, and by his ignorance of th e targeted child payment
created by my bill. I urge New Zealanders to take this step for children and to join our
Green Party campaign to end child poverty, to  become champions for children, and to
make poverty a political issue so that no politic ian could ever turn their face away from
the facts or the solutions—to make it such a political issue that even John Key could not
reject those children who go hungry, who go cold, while he has his holidays and plays
his golf on “Planet Key”.
I urge the House to send this bill to the select committee to allow the debate to be
had as to what kind of support we should be providing to families and children and how
we might best do it. All New Zealand childre n deserve a good life and a fair future, but
we cannot deny that for many thousands life is  not great. It is a cold and hungry place,
New Zealand. So let us make New Zealand a great place to grow up for every single
New Zealand child and do that tonight. I commend this bill to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and speak on this
bill, the Income Tax (Universalisation of In-work Tax Credit) Amendment Bill. I want
to start by paying tribute to Metiria Turia b ecause I do believe that  she has brought this
to—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. That is a deliberate
mispronunciation.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I hope it was not deliberate.
Pronunciation is a very important thing and some people do have difficulty with it, but I
would hope that the member does his best.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: I apologise; it was not intentional.  If it was intentional it would
have been much, much longer than that, but  I thank the member opposite for correcting
me on that.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: It may have been your accent, Todd.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: It must have been my accent—ex actly. I want to pay tribute to
the member—Ms Turia?

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Turei.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: Turei—hooray! I got it right. I pay tribute to Ms Turei for
bringing this bill to the House. The reason for that is th at I do believe she has brought it
here with good intention. But, having said that, it is not something the Government can
support, and the reason for that  is we do not believe that th is legislation will achieve
anything close to what she actually wants to achieve with it.
The Government is committed to investing in ways to eliminate child hardship and
improve the economic and social well-being of individuals, families, and communities.
17 Oct 2012 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 5959
We are doing that through supporting families and indi viduals into work and,
importantly, recognising those families who do work. I think this legislation would blur
those lines about what we need to do in th is country and what is achievable for those
who deserve support to be able to do more for themselves.
The welfare reforms that we have introduced and the measures that we are taking to
support New Zealand families will ensure that we are getting New Zealanders off
benefits and into work, where they are much  better off. I challenge members of this
House to find examples of where families who work are not better off—every member
of the family being better off. On this side of the House we are committed to fairness
and an unrelenting focus on work, and we are focused on what people can do, not on
what they cannot do.

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: This is jargon now.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: It is what New Zealanders voted for at the last election. It is a
commitment and a promise we made, and one we are delivering on.
This bill, from a member of the Green Party, seeks to pay people to stay on benefits,
rather than supporting working families. I will  say that again: it seeks to pay people to
stay on benefits, rather than supporting them into jobs and into work. There is a very
important difference in philosophy between th e two sides of the House. You see, the
current in-work tax credit offers an incentive for people with families to gain and retain
sustainable employment, helping to ensure a better living standard and a secure future
for them and for their families. Evidence suggests that the most effective way to achieve
a long-term, sustainable reduction in child hard ship is to address its causes directly by
encouraging and helping people into work, wh ile continuing to provide support in the
shorter term.
This is about making sure that we suppor t those people. As a society and as a
Government we absolutely must support thos e on welfare, who need the assistance of
their society, but we also need to take re sponsibility to help them to do more for
themselves and for their families. I do not be lieve that this bill will achieve that.
Evidence suggests that the most effective way to achieve a l ong-term, sustainable
reduction in child poverty is to  address its causes directly by encouraging and assisting
people into paid work, while continuing to provide that support in the short term.
I want to touch upon some of the things th at we have been doing in this area. The
issue of children, how they are raised, wh at support is available to them, and their
livelihood around them is extremely important to us in Government, and I do take it that
it is important to all members of the House. Where we are different is the approach to
how we combat this problem. The Government  is committed to investing in ways to
eliminate child hardship and to improve the lives of individuals, families, and
communities, both economically and socially. Some of the changes to welfare reform
that we are putting in place currently through this House are a step in that direction.
The Ministerial Committee on Poverty is working through a number of issues critical
to improving the lives of low-income New Zealanders and their families. This
committee is focusing on ensuring that the Government is getting results from the
billions of dollars it spends on a wide range of social services. I will say that again: the
billions of dollars that it spends on a wide  range of social services. We are able to
commit and spend that money to support New Zealanders who deserve support only
because hard-working other New Zealanders ar e out paying their taxes. Where we can
encourage people and help them into the wo rkforce, they and their families, their
children, are better off. The Government has invested in increasing our knowledge
about the nature, extent, and persistence of  material hardship amongst families with
dependent children in New Zealand, and we  are committed to continuing to make
progress on eliminating this hardship where it exists in New Zealand.
5960 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 17 Oct 2012

items.speaker: I hear members opposite say
items.text: “Where are the jobs? Where are the jobs?”. We are
hearing that a lot, but 60,000 jobs were created by this Government—60,000 jobs have
been created. Members opposite might not like that, members opposite may be
disappointed by that, but the cold, hard truth and the f act is that jobs ha ve been created.
What we do have a challenge with in this country is people who do not have the skills to
be able to fill these jobs as they are created. It is a very  important piece of work the
Government is doing to look to support them, to help them, to bring more skills to them,
and to give them confidence and at the same time skills, so that they can find their way
to the workforce.
We make no apologies for saying that familie s are better off when a member of their
household works. It is an overarching amb ition and a challenge, and the direction the
Government is going in is to help more New Zealanders into the workforce. Again—I
come back to where I started—to the me mber who has sponsored  this bill: I do
recognise that she is concerned about the hardship of children and families in New
Zealand, and I think there are many areas where we will be able to work with other
parties in this Parliament to find ongoing soluti ons to these problems. Unfortunately, I
do not believe that this bill is one of those solutions, and therefore the Government will
not be supporting it.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I found that speech from the member Todd
McClay, quite frankly, offensive. The implica tion from that side of  the House that we
hear continually is that somehow members on this side of the House, all of the
Opposition members, do not have an intere st in improving the lives of children,
particularly those who are in the homes of people on Government support; this notion
that we pay to keep people on welfare rather than trying to move them into work, where
apparently everything in life gets better when you are on a meagre minimum wage.
Well, I have news for that side of the House: 40 percent of the children living in
poverty at the moment are in the homes of  people who are working. They are the
working poor. If you want to improve the lives of children in the homes of families who
are already in work, you could start by lifting the minimum wage.
This bill, the Income Tax (Universalisati on of In-work Tax Credit) Amendment Bill,
is about poverty. That side of the House is ignoring that it is not just about those who
are on Government support. Even in work, fa milies are struggling. And that side of the
House has tried to claim that there is not any incentive in this country to be in work. Do
you know what the best incentive that we currently have is? How much, Mr McClay,
does a sole parent on the DP B receive? How much does a sole parent on the domestic
purposes benefit receive?

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: How many kids?

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: With one child. With one child, what is the main benefit
rate—the main benefit rate—for the DPB? I h ear silence. That, Mr McClay, is the best
incentive we have to move into work. We  pay $293 to a sole parent on the DPB. And
what do we pay a 20-year-old on the unemp loyment benefit? Anyone? Anyone on that
side of the House? I will take offers. It is $170.
It is time we broke through the rhetoric. On that side of the House there is a constant
implication that people are making a choice— a lifestyle choice—to be on Government
support, that they live in the lap of luxury, and that  they are making poor and
irresponsible choices on behalf  of their children. In most cases—in the vast majority of
cases—that is simply not the case. They do not have the means to provide well for their
children. And the longer that that Government  spins rhetoric that it is solely about
parental responsibility, all it is trying to do is take responsib ility off itself to provide an
environment where there are opportunities; where families are able to move into decent,
sustainable, well-paying jobs; and where sole parents who are primary carers are able to
17 Oct 2012 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 5961
provide adequately for their children when th ey have no choice but to  be the carer and,
in fact, when that is the best place for them to be in that vulnerable stage of that child’s
life.
That Government is disowning responsibil ity for an issue that  is affecting 270,000
children. Let us not desensitise the issue. This  is not just a number; these are kids who
are, as Metiria Turei has said, going to school without food in  their bellies and shoes on
their feet. And this Government implies that  this is simply a state of irresponsible
parenting. It goes well beyond that, and any attempt to detract from the issue in that way
is an insult to the children who are affected by it.
Let us look at this Government’s record wh en it comes to child poverty. It dismissed
the Expert Advisory Group on Solutions to Child Poverty’s recommendations on
increasing incomes for children in poverty. It called them “dopey”. It dismissed
Labour’s policy of food in school s, saying that fruit in sc hools was surely enough. It
even dismissed my bill, which was simply about setting measurements for poverty and
subsequent targets. This is a Government that has no political will to address child
poverty.
This bill should be going to select comm ittee. Labour, when in Government, lifted
over 100,000 children out of poverty through Working for Families. But we are quite
honest; we left unfinished business. Last elec tion one of the policies we put forward as
an idea to address this was the extensio n of the in-work tax credit. We have not
removed that policy from the table, but we ha ve been very open that we are looking at
alternatives to see whether there is another and better way to increase the incomes of the
households with children who are in desper ate poverty, and we will continue on that
search.
But until that point we will be supporting this  bill. This Government should too, if it
wants to prove that it has any political will to address an issue that is costing all of us
dearly, not least children.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: It was interesting to hear the previous speaker,
Jacinda Ardern, suggest that she was offended by what this House was saying. I am not
so easily offended, but there is a constant refrain that comes from that side of the House
that this side of the House does not care about people and it does not care about
children. Well, frankly, I find that offensiv e. The reason why this Government is
moving ahead with welfare reform is precisely  that the current regime, which we have
had for the last few decades, is not working e ffectively. We do it because we need to do
it for the sake of the children of this country.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Labour had 9 years.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: And it has had a long time. I ju st want to start off with a
couple of quotes because what we seem to be boiling down to here this evening is
diverging views about the impor tance of work. I will quote he re from Metiria Turei in
this House on the first day of  this session where she talked  about the Prime Minister
restating the myth “that work is a path out of poverty. The truth is that it is not.” This is

items.speaker: Mrs Turei speaking
items.text: “For the two in ever y five children who live in poverty whose
parents work, work is not the pathway out of poverty. Work is the trap, because work is
not properly paid.” There you have that as tounding comment from the Greens, whose
members do not believe that work is the way out of poverty.
I recently came across a quote from Frank lin Delano Roosevelt in 1935. It is an
interesting quote, I thought , from the man who probably more than anybody started
welfarism in this country, for those who do not know their history. He said: “Continued
dependence on government support induces a spiritual and moral disintegration
fundamentally destructive to the national fibr e. To dole out relief in this way is to
administer a narcotic, a subtle destroyer of the human spirit.” Well, I am not sure what
5962 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 17 Oct 2012
to make of both those comments, but the point that I am making is that this side of the
House believes that work is a good thing, an d the whole point of the Government’s
activities and proposals in its welfare activities and its gr owth promotion and the way
that it focuses on building the economy is because  we believe that it is best for children
to be raised in households where people work  and find meaning in their lives for earned
success. We go back to Michael Joseph Savage in this country promising that he would
end poverty with the welfare State in New Z ealand, and 70 years later we still have
more of it.
So this National Government is committed to investing in ways that eliminate child
hardship and improve the economic and soci al well-being of individuals, but our
welfare reforms are measures taken to suppor t New Zealand families to ensure we are
getting New Zealanders out of benefits and into work, where they are so much better
off. On this side of the House we are committed to fairness and an unrelenting and
unapologetic focus on work. We are focused on what people can do, not what they
cannot do. We do not accept that it  is a good thing for a child to be raised in a house
where nobody has worked for generations. Th e essence of this bill and the Greens’
policy is just to somehow think that the problem will be solved by giving yet more and
extending benefits, when we should be focusing on finding ways to encourage people to
get back to work, which is what this Governme nt is all about. I am af raid we all in this
House agree that child poverty is an issue for this country. It is that we disagree on how
best to remedy that, and this bill, unfortuna tely, is not, in my view, one that would
remedy it at all in the long term. Thank you.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First) : Malo le soifua i lau
susuga. The Income Tax (Universalisation of In-work Tax Credit) Amendment Bill
proposes to amend changes to the criteria in the Working for Families package by
removing discriminatory elements that are a ttached to the in-work tax credit. The bill
intends to assist vulnerable children, and that is a good thing—it is a good thing. So Mr
McClay’s misinterpretation of this bill is a real concern. To say that it is to pay people
to stay on welfare is astonishing, in my view. My advice to Mr McClay is this: he needs
to do some exercise, and the only thing he  should exercise is caution—caution, Mr
McClay. No one was born to be a bad citi zen. Exposing them to risk and unhealthy
environments contributes to the negative outcomes that the National Government has
been creating in the last 4 years.
This package is supposed to support families with children on low and middle
incomes, and it is worth $60 per week. Is that right, Ms Turei? It is $60 per week for
poor families with one to three children and an additional $15 per week for each
additional child. However, there are implications. [ Interruption] It is week ly? All right.
OK. However, there are implications in this package regarding parents who do not meet
the threshold for working hours—and I am talking about the 30 hours between a couple.
Parents who receive income-tested benefits and parents who receive a student allowance
will get $60 per week less in the current framework of the Working for Families
package because of their eligibility under the IWTC, or the in-work tax credit.
The proposed amendments to the in-work tax credit are based on elements of the
Working for Families package that discriminate on the basis of parental work status. It
does discriminate. So this bill aims to am end the Income Tax Act 2007 to capture all
children of beneficiaries, students, and families under the in-work tax credit. The
proposed amendments would require the cr iteria under the Working for Families
package to emphasise income, rather than work—income, rather than work. Income and
work are both interrelated, but if parents are unable to meet the requirement to work 20
to 30 hours per week and their reasons are justified in some wa y, then the package
17 Oct 2012 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 5963
should recognise this, rather than turning a blind eye to the actuali ties that people are
confronted with.
There are also issues surrounding high unemp loyment periods, where it is difficult
for parents to find work. Work is something that has become a foreign environment on
that side of the House.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: Very good speech!
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : It is. If changes do not occur,
children will continue to suffer at the hands of the system, and that will contribute to
greater poverty rates in the future. The estim ated cost of the bill is around $300 million
annually, which is a very small amount compar ed with the $6 billi on annually to target
poverty. This bill will invest in the future of our children and will contribute to a more
equal society.
New Zealand First will support this bill’s re ferral to the Social  Services Committee.
Let the people of New Zealand have their say. It is time that democracy was given a fair
opportunity to be exercised in this House. Thank you.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: That was actually quite a
reasonable speech from New Zealand First. I was quite surprised and I thought it was
pretty good from those members. But let us ha ve a look at what we are dealing with in
this House tonight.
This bill, the Income Tax (Universalisati on of In-work Tax Credit) Amendment Bill,
is not so much about work. This is about increasing the welfare State or providing—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: It’s about communism!

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: That is what this is about. That is what the Labour and the
Green parties are about. They come to this House and they play holier than thou. They
stand up and they say that the Government doe s not care about children, that we do not
have a heart, that we do not make the right decisions, that they do, that they are standing
on some pedestal, and that they know what is right. What they are actually doing,
though—the Labour Party and the Green Party,  and the New Zealand First Party—is

The National Government is doing the right th ings to build an economy that delivers
the solutions. The solution is not giving more  money to people so that those members
can say that they have taken them out of poverty. I ask members of this House: are there
members of our communities who are on benefits who are not in poverty?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Yes, there are.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: There are. There will be. There will be people who can manage
their benefit to provide food for their childre n, who can provide a roof over their head,
and who can provide shoes on their feet. Not all people on a benefit are in poverty. That

What we are doing here is we are looki ng for a solution thr ough welfare—a solution

place giving $60 to certain families. That wi ll not take those families out of poverty,
will it?
5964 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 17 Oct 2012

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Yes, it will.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Is $60 going to be enough? Sixty dollars is all the Labour Party
says we need to give to beneficiaries to  take them out of poverty. Well, how about
working people, then, who earn more than bene ficiaries and are still in poverty? Does it
take them out of poverty? No, it cannot. How can the Green Party say that $60 will take
people out of poverty, and yet working peopl e who earn more have still got poverty
with the $60? How does it work? Is that the Russel Norman approach to economics? Is
it based on his theo ries? No. It is not true . It is not going to wo rk. It is not going to
achieve the purpose. Do not come into this  House and try to say to the Government:
“You’re mean. You don’t care.” Do not pr ey on people’s emotions to put your
arguments across. That is all that the Green Party is trying to do.
This is the Green Party, the Green Party that, before the last election, said: “We
never do personal attacks.” Its members went on TV and said: “We’re bigger than that.
We never do personal attacks.” Here tonight,  what does a co-leader of the Green Party
do in her speech? A personal attack on the Prim e Minister. It is all the Green Party can
do. Stick to the knitting, look at what you s hould do as a green party, and do not try to
change the economic framework of the world.  To the voters out there, be aware. The
Green Party does not put up bills about helping our rivers and our lakes; it puts up bills
about spending other people’s money, and that is  all that it would ever do if it got into
Government. The Green Party is all about soci al reform and it is all about spending
other people’s money. It is a classic left-wing party; it is not a real green party. Those
members should be ashamed to call themselves that and to be in this House under that
name.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): Talofa lava, Mr Speaker. I found that
last speech quite patronising, and I believe th at that speaker, David Bennett, is blind to
the poverty that exists in hi s electorate in Hamilton. I want to welcome the introduction
of this bill, the Income Tax (Universalisat ion of In-work Tax Credit) Amendment Bill,
by Metiria Turei, as an opportunity to deba te and discuss the issue of poverty that many
families—beneficiary families and working families, including middle-income
families—are now facing, especially familie s that have young children. We need to
really talk about what we do with the 270,000 children who are living in abject poverty
in New Zealand. We in Labour are totally committed to reducing child poverty, and we
are looking at a range of ways to achieve this. Extending the in-work tax credit in the
way that this bill introduces is only one of those ways. That  has been part of our policy
in the last election, and it is part of our goal to try to reduce child poverty. That is a goal
that we remain absolutely committed to, and as part of our policy process we are
looking through a range of opt ions, including the opti ons that the Children’s
Commissioner’s Expert Advisory Group on Solu tions to Child Poverty has thrown up.
We are going to consider those, because we know it is a real problem, and we believe
that if we do not tackle it now, it will be dire for the future of Aotearoa New Zealand.
David Shearer has also rolled out Labour’s commitment to ensure that children are
not learning while hungry in decile 1 to 3 primary and in termediate schools. We have
pledged to work with community groups to provide free food in every decile 1 to 3
primary and intermediate school that need s and wants it. Of course parents are
responsible for looking after their kids, but th at will not change th e reality that some
children are turning up to school hungry, turn ing up to school without shoes, and their
learning is affected, and that  should be unacceptable to all of us. Labour makes no
apology for committing funding for the sake of ou r children. I think that we have got to
commit ourselves for the sake of our children.
There have been an additional 30,000 ch ildren living in benefit-dependent
households since this Government came in to power. Again, this  is unacceptable.
17 Oct 2012 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 5965
According to an OECD report, New Zeala nd has one of the highe st rates of child
poverty, and one of the lowest levels of investment in the first 5 years of life, among the
34 OECD countries. Again, this should be to tally unacceptable to all of us. Research
shows that poverty and income inadequacy  are key drivers of poor outcomes for
children. There is a need for more houses, qua lity and warmer homes, especially in
Christchurch, and they have to be affordable  for all. We have got to be prepared to
acknowledge that there is poverty and be prep ared to measure progress of what we do
about it. It is unacceptable for any Government—any Government—to allow significant
numbers of people to live in  persistent poverty. The numbe r of children living in
hardship has increased from  15 percent in 2007 to 21 pe rcent last ye ar. It is
unacceptable, I say, for any Prime Mini ster—any Prime Minister—to promise
incessantly during an election campaign a brig hter future for all New Zealanders, and
then fail to deliver after he got everyone to buy into that promise. Every New Zealander,
I would say, would be disappoi nted, and has every right to be, in the failure of this
Government to keep that promise.
Once upon a time there was no poverty—not the kind of poverty that we see today.
People had jobs. People were well paid. Most families could generally have one person
working. Everyone had a house that was afford able, everyone had food on their table,
milk was delivered to people’s doorsteps, ev eryone had a family doctor, education was
free, and as a country we collectively looked af ter one another. We came together.
Everybody pulled together, did their bit, and af terwards we celebrated over a barbecue.
That was the New Zealand way. That was the Kiwi way, and sadly we have lost that. I
have to blame, to a large extent, this G overnment being in power and the kinds of
policies that it is introducing. I want to say to National members that they have got to
recognise that there is a real problem, a nd unless they do that, nothing is going to be
done under this Government’s watch. Labour a nd Shearer will fight to ensure that we
get rid of the poverty.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: As the Green Party spokesperson  for income support, it is an
absolute pleasure to speak to this Income Tax (Universalisation of In-work Tax Credit)
Amendment Bill. This legislation will actua lly do something, pretty much immediately,
to reduce child poverty if it is introduced, and all without stigmatising anyone. It is like
a miracle. Of course, it will not fix everythi ng, but it will make an immediate tangible
difference, and that is more than any other idea I have heard in this House recently. As a
country, we can find the money to make sure everyone has a good life and a fair future,
if we just make the commitment to do it— and that is not a Communist conspiracy.
Extending the in-work tax credit would cost between $300 million to $400 million a
year. Child poverty is estimated to cost this economy over $6 billion a year. The
benefits of extending the child payment are more than the costs, no matter which way
you look at it. Metiria has already outlined  several compelling reasons for supporting
her legislation. I would now like to add just  a couple more. The primary one for me is
that benefit levels are just too low and th e consequences of child poverty are far too
high.
Now I would like to bring in some of the words of young people and their
experiences of poverty, as found by the Children’s Commissioner.  This is their view of
what it is to live in poverty in New Zealand: “You get sick easily. Being left out. Not
having enough money. Shame, neglect, lack of  warm clothing. Livi ng week to week.
Not accepted by your peers. Debts. Phone and elect ricity cut off. Hard to fit in and take
part in things like sport. Going without n ecessities. Moving a lot.  Scary and stressful.
Bad housing, overcrowding. Can’t go on school trips. Choices you can’t make, choices
taken away. Lack of warm clothing. Can’t afford to go to the doctors. Cold, grotty
disgusting housing. Not enough food. Hungry. Can’t afford school uniforms. Get picked
5966 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 17 Oct 2012
on at school. Missed opportunities. Feeling of worthlessness. No good clothes. Getting
pick on or bullied. Sad, disappointed, frustr ated, angry. Children paying the price for
parents’ mistakes. Lack of school books and stationery.”
I have heard the Government’s view that the way to improve child outcomes is to get
their parents into paid work, and of course th is has an instinctive appeal to pretty much
everyone because actually we all want to wo rk. But there are three problems with this.
One is that parenting is work; two, there need s to be paid work to  get into; and, three,
child outcomes improve only when the parents ar e in reasonably paid jobs with decent
conditions and flexibility, and there is plenty of research to back that up that I am happy
to provide to any member of this House. Our benefit system even tacitly acknowledges
that. For sole parents with children under 14, their focus may need to be on the care of
their children. Despite the erosion of this principle in the new welfare reforms, our
welfare system still retains this core value. Full-time work expectations kick in only
when the youngest child is 14,  so this Government even  acknowledges that parenting
for children under that age is work and should be able to be a focus, and yet it refuses to
allow an increase in income to those families and to those children.
Finally, I would like to finish with a poem from a student from Ōtāhuhu:
Poverty is just a word …
but a word that means a lot
not when said
but when seen.
Poverty is just a cycle
but an on-going cycle
not being altered
but left aside.
Poverty is on our conscience
but at the back of our minds
not acted on …
but why not?
“PLEEZZE To people in power + the G overnment—don’t tuck us away as a
statistic.”

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: I rise to speak to the Income Tax
(Universalisation of In-work Tax Credit) Amendment Bill. Even the name is ridiculous.
It is, of course, a natural extension for a pa rty that wants to prin t money, put us on the
path that Zimbabwe is on, and make us th e richest country on the planet. Quantitative
easing—literally printing money—is a flawed no tion for a party that thinks it is helping
out people who are poor. It is very consistent  with the bill it has put up now, which we
utterly oppose. Perhaps I will come back to  quantitative easing, because there is so
much to say about it.
I would like to firstly outline why we are against the bill. The John Key National-led
Government is committed to investing in wa ys to eliminate child hardship and to
improve the economic and social well-being of individuals, families, and communities.
This is a bill that would work against that. Our welfare reforms and the measures we are
taking to support New Zealand fa milies are going to  absolutely ensure that we will get
New Zealanders off benefits and into work, wh ere they will be much better off, instead
of leaving them imprisoned in a benefit sy stem. On this side of the House we are
committed to fairness and an unrelenting focus on work. This is what people do, if they
can. Being on benefits, being cocooned, bei ng on “Cloud Green”, or whatever you are
calling yourselves these days, is  a ridiculous thing—as ridicu lous as the name of this
17 Oct 2012 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 5967
bill and the notion that underpin s it. This is a bill from th e Greens that seeks to pay
people to stay on benefits, rather  than support working families. [ Interruption] Of
course it is. There are none so blind as those who do not see.
Let us go back to one of the favourite things  that Dr Norman put out last week about
quantitative easing. I mean, how ridiculous—hi tting the poor the hardest. If you printed
money in the way that Zimbabwe does, and Dr Norman and his band of merry Greens
would have us do, then everybody who goes to the supermarket, goes to the petrol
pump, goes to buy children’s clothing will have to pay more. So what is the point of
that? How is that going to relieve child poverty and hardship within families? It will
make it worse. The 1+1=2 scenario is lost on the Greens. Arithmetically they are utterly
challenged, and this is yet further proof of it.
I looked through this bill. The current in-work tax credit, which is offering currently
an incentive for people with families to gain and retain sustainable employment, is also
helping to ensure a better living standard and to secure a future for them and their
families—not borrow, borrow, borrow, get furt her into debt, get indebted not just for
this generation but for future generations. Again, it is the printing money thing. You
know, we should remind ourselves about the “Watermelon Greens”—green on the
outside and bright red to the core. It is a very socialist—and that is putting it mildly—
measure that they come out with repeatedl y. It is nonsense. So I am very proud to be
part of a Government that does not support it in any way, shape, or form.
Let us look at some of the evidence, sh all we? I mean, this is something you
probably cannot google in 2 minut es, which is what the Green s and their research unit
tend to go in for, rather than substantive ev idence and substantive proof. It is just kind
of what they do, really. So let us look at the evidence. It suggests that the most effective
way to achieve a long-term—not just a shor t-term, little, tiny, Green-minded one, but a
long-term one—sustained reduction in child po verty is to address the causes directly,
and that is why encouraging and assisting pe ople into paid work while continuing to
provide support in the short term is targeted. The pained expressions, the unbelieving
faces of the Greens! They really do not get it, and maybe they never will. But we will
certainly not be voting in favour of this bill.
I am very proud to be part of a Government that in fact does things that really make
the future secure for our children, grandc hildren, and great-grandchildren. We care
about the environment. The Greens purport to. How many questions do they ever ask in
the House about the environment? There is the odd one on fracking, the Māui’s dolphin,
one or two on—what is your favourite, Ms Logie? Sex-change people going into
prisons. There has been a lot of  talk of these fringe issu es. And the other stuff they
prattle on about? Well, it is  about the economy, because Dr Norman wants to be the
next Minister of Finance, if the unholy allia nce of Labour and the Gr eens ever actually
makes it across the line.  I fervently hope they do not, fo r the sake of New Zealand and
our long-term future.
There is an international consensus, t oo, that the Greens tend to miss out on. The
medical community knows and understands—our esteemed Minister of Health, the Hon
Tony Ryall, does as well—the general health benefits. People’s recovery from illness or
injury is improved. To be in an environmen t where there is not be nefit dependency is a
good thing. Thank you.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.

POINTS OF ORDER 
Motions, Members’—Process for Debating 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First) : I raise a point of order, Mr 
Speaker. Is there a process to have my  motion, which was submitted in time this 
morning, debated? In view of its importance, when? 
Mr SPEAKER: It will be set down tomorrow as a members’ order of the day, which 
is the normal process. 
Hon David Parker—Statement Regarding Withdrawal from Chamber 
Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour): Mr Speaker.  
Mr SPEAKER: The Hon David Parker, point of order.  
Hon DAVID PARKER: No, Mr Speaker. Mr Speaker. 
Mr SPEAKER: Does the member wish to raise a point of order?  
Hon DAVID PARKER: How can the Speaker know that, until I call— 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! There is no question—[ Interruption] Order! There is no 
question in front of the House, so if the me mber seeks the Speaker’s call, he must be 
raising a point of order. I have sufficient—[ Interruption] Goodness! I have sufficient 
courtesy for members to treat them with that kind of courtesy. Where there is no 
question in front of the House, if a member ge ts to their feet, they  are clearly raising a 
point of order, and I recognise d the member on that basis.  Does the member wish to 
raise a point of order?  
Hon DAVID PARKER: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Yes, I do wish to raise 
a point of order. Mr Speaker, for the first time in 10 years I was ejected from this 
Parliament yesterday, and I did not even ha ve the opportunity to put a point of order 
before you ejected me. I want you to note that point. [Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! We all have our foibles. 
Motions, Members’—Process for Debating 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First) : I raise a point of order, Mr 
Speaker. My question to you was whether there is a process in respect of that motion; 
not whether it appears in the business of the House tomorrow, but what the process is 
thereafter, particularly—[Interruption]

2. ANDREW WILLIAMS (NZ First)  to the Member in charge of the Reserve 
Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primar y Function of Bank) Amendment Bill : 
What are the flaws in the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989 that the Reserve 
Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment Bill seeks to 
address? 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Member in ch arge of the Reserve Bank of New 
Zealand (Amending Primary Func tion of Bank) Amendment Bill) : Another 
superbly drafted question. The current Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act puts 
unwarranted emphasis on price stability, and does not allow the Reserve Bank to pursue 
a broad mandate for economic policy that covers growth, exports, and jobs. The original 
Act, of course, was to try to combat the dogs of inflation unleashed by the neo-liberals

in this country—much subscribed to by the present administration. The focus on 
inflation in the current Act, to the neglect of other important economic indicators—

well in all that time—has lead to a chr onically overvalued exchange rate, which is 
seriously undermining New Zealand’s international competitiveness. 
Andrew Williams : Why is it necessary to broaden the primary functions of the 
Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989 as this bill proposes?

longer fit for purpose in the current econom ic era. The general consensus among 
economic commentators is that in the wa ke of the global financial crisis the

inflation, along with the intense efforts by many countries  to hold the value of their

3. ANDREW WILLIAMS (NZ First)  to the Member in charge of the Reserve 
Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primar y Function of Bank) Amendment Bill : 
What other functions will the Reserve Bank of New Zeala nd (Amending Primary 
Function of Bank) Amendment Bill seek to include in section 8 of the principal Act? 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Member in ch arge of the Reserve Bank of New 
Zealand (Amending Primary Functi on of Bank) Amendment Bill) : The Reserve 
Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment Bill will 
allow the bank to incorporate into its monetary policy the goal of achieving a stable and 
competitive exchange rate, an d all over provincial New Ze aland they cannot wait for 
this bill to pass. The bill will enable the appropriate authority and importance to be 
attached to economic growth and employme nt, as well as the desperately needed 
promotion of exports in an export-dependent nation. 
Andrew Williams: What would the latest CPI figur es mean for the Reserve Bank if 
the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Amendi ng Primary Function of Bank) Amendment 
Bill became law? 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS: That is a very apposite question. If the Reserve Bank 
of New Zealand (Amending Primary Functi on of Bank) Amendment Bill was treated 
seriously by serious legislators, and not jeered at because of neo-liberal antagonism, and 
became law, it would mean that the bank could take a full account of prevailing 
economic conditions—that is, that inflation no longer needs to be the primary target and 
the only imperative of economic policy. The Reserve Bank would, as an example, be 
better able to take into account the latest CPI figures in formulating a rational monetary 
policy that met New Zealand’s broader econom ic policy objectives. If a man as bright 
as Lee Kuan Yew could see the sense in this, I wonder why those members cannot.

I move, That the Mount Maunganui Borough Reclamation and Empowering Act 
Repeal Bill be now read a second time . The Mount Maunganui Borough Reclamation 
and Empowering Act Repeal Bill is an important  bill on two counts, if I can start that 
way. Firstly, there is a local nawe, an issue of local concern to the people of Rangataua 
Bay and, more broadly, across Tauranga Moan a. The second note of significance is the 
national picture—how the legacy of this b ill will, we hope, influence greater power-
sharing with Māori right across the motu.  
If I can turn your attention firstly to the local perspective, and give some background 
to those listening, this bill repeals th e Mount Maunganui Borough Reclamation and 
Empowering Act 1975, so it has been around for a while. The area we focused on in the 
bill was taken by the Mount Maunganui Borough Council for the purposes of 
5912 Mt Maunganui Reclamation & Empowering Act Repeal Bill 17 Oct 2012 
establishing sewage ponds at the eas tern end of Rangataua Bay, Te T āhuna o 
Rangataua, in my electorate of Waiariki, and in the Tauranga area. In essence, the 1975 
Act gave the Bay of Plenty Harbour Board the au thority to transfer part of the seabed of 
Tauranga Harbour to the Mount Maunganui Bo rough Council, and then, to add insult to 
injury, authorised the council to  undertake reclamation of th at part of the harbour for 
sewerage and other purposes.  
Ngā Pōtiki, as the local iwi, and individuals like the late W īremu Ōhia, Chair of the 
Tauranga Moana M āori Executive, and Paraone R ēweti, the MP for Eastern M āori at 
the time, were very, very vocal in protesti ng that the area was a source of food for the 
people and had an important hi story attached to it. In the submission to the Local 
Government and Environment Committee, their point of view is clearly outlined, and I 
quote from the submission: “For Nga Potiki and indeed Tauranga Maori, the discharge 
of human waste into the pristine Te Tahuna o Rangataua, that had served as a pataka kai 
… for centuries was and remains utterly repugnant.” So you can understand that 
Tauranga people were not happy.  
What was particular ly disturbing for Ng ā Pōtiki was that the outfa ll pipe was going 
to head to the ocean by way of an urup ā and wāhi tapu—in other words, a cemetery and 
some sacred sites. This was their ancestral  landscape, confirmed by the awards of the 
Papamoa Block to Ng ā Pōtiki by the Crown commissioners  in the late 1880s. During 
the select committee, what I f ound of particular interest was that the objec tions of that 
day were not voiced just by M āori alone. Indeed, the Mini stry of Agriculture and 
Fisheries and the Ministry of Transport also opposed the proposal to reclaim the 
foreshore and the seabed. At the same time, an environmental impact report established 
in 1974 concluded that “a flourishing ecosy stem on the tidal flats would be lost” 
through reclamation. The Parliamentary Comm issioner for the Envi ronment concluded 
that the reclamation could not be justifie d, because of the impact on the area and the 
possibility of other sites being used. So all parties, if you want to put it that way, were 
agreed that this was an area of significant environmental and cultural value. Yet, despite 
all of these objections, the Parliament of the day went ahead anyway. And 37 years on, 
here we are, and we are finally listening to  the wisdom of those who have gone before 
us.  
It has not just happened ove rnight, and I want to firs tly acknowledge those people 
who some 13 years ago started taking direct action to restore the land to its essence. I 
want to be clear that the relationship that we are repairing in this legislation is not just 
between mana whenua and the respective c ouncil; it is actually also about Ng ā Pōtiki 
and its close relationship to the land—in par ticular, Te T āhuna o Rangataua. We are 
recognising a history honoured through oral  tradition, through waiata, pepeha, and 
whakataukī, proverbs.  
This relationship was constantly referred to in the evidence submitted by Ng ā Pōtiki 
kaumātua to the Waitangi Tribunal held at Ma ngatawa Marae in 1999. At that time, the 
people unanimously resolved to estab lish the trust to be known as the Ng ā Pōtiki-a-
Tamapāhore Trust to represent and advocate Ng ā Pōtiki’s interests with the Crown. In 
2000 the Tauranga City Council started a consultation process, establishing the Tangata 
Whenua Tauranga City Council Standing Comm ittee to facilitate improved engagement 
between Māori and the council. Four years later the Tauranga  Moana Tangata Whenua 
Collective was established, bringing togeth er representatives of all 15 iwi and hap ū 
resident within the boundaries of Tauranga  City Council. Thirteen of the 15 have 
protocol agreements with the council, which outline how they will work together.  
 So if we fast track back from then to th is bill, I want to commend the Tauranga City 
Council for its recognition that although it has inherited an area th at is still being 
utilised, a significant portion of the land originally taken will not be needed, and so it

has moved to hand it back to the people—awes ome. For me it is great to see that the 
council and iwi are working together, and I cannot work out how this has not happened 
far more often. When it does happen, it us ually removes the angst by iwi, hap ū, and 
whānau about not being engaged and involved in decision making as tangata whenua,

And I have to say how great it was to read the submission—and there was only one

Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green): I rise to speak on the Reserve Bank 
of New Zealand (Amending Primary Functio n of Bank) Amendment Bill, which is 
looking at changing some of the monetary policy settings for New Zealand. The reason 
why this debate is important is that the greatest challenge facing the New Zealand 
economy at the moment is the external imbalances.  
What the Government is either oblivious to or is trying to downplay is the fact that 
New Zealand is currently running a 5 pe rcent of GDP curren t account deficit—5 
percent, or $10 billion a year. Under the Rese rve Bank projections it is expected to 
increase to closer to 7 percent. This is a major problem for New Zealand, and the reason 
it is a problem is that there are only two wa ys to pay for a current account deficit. The 
first is to borrow more money, and New Zeal and already has a very large problem with 
overseas debt, and the second is to sell more assets.  
As people who have followed the debate in New Zealand will know, we have sold 
off large numbers of New Zealand assets in to foreign ownership over the last 25 years 
in order to cover a chronic current account de ficit. If we do not deal with the current 
account deficit, then, fundamentally, we will undermine our long-term prosperity 
because we will rack up more and more international debt, and we will have to service 
that debt, and we will sell off more and more of our assets into overseas ownership—
both the land and the companies—and we will lose the profits from those companies 
overseas.  
We know, when we speak to actual exporters , that one of the major problems that 
they face is around the dollar.  This is both in the farmi ng sector—the most recent 
Rabobank survey found that the overvalued exchange rate was a problem—and it is also 
across the board in manufacturing, where we have lost 40,000 jobs in the 4 years to 
June 2012.  
The overvalued dollar is driven in large part, but only in part, by the monetary policy 
that New Zealand has run for the last 20 year s, and that, effectively, has been a high 
exchange rate and a high interest rate pol icy. In the current context, where other 
countries are involved in competitive deva luations, that has cr eated an enormous 
problem for New Zealand that has exacerbated the pre-existing current account deficits. 
That is why it is so essential that we do something about it.  
We have heard from the Government that what people who want a lower exchange 
rate want is to increase the price of flat-screen TVs, and this is clearly the Government’s 
populist appeal, I guess, against changing monetary policy setti ngs. The thing is that if 
we do not deal with our current account defi cit, we have a long-term economic problem 
where we increase debt and we lose ownership of the New Zealand economy.  
So when the Government makes short-term  appeals and says to people: “Oh, the 
Government will keep a high exchange rate . Sure we will have to fund everything 
through borrowed money, but your flat-scr een TVs will be cheap.”, that is the

Government’s economic strategy, and that is the Government’s political strategy. It 
wants to be popular by having a high New Ze aland dollar, so that  imports are cheap. 
This has been the Government’s argument  time and again around monetary policy. But 
we should be clear. Sure, imports will be cheap er in the short term, but the way we will

Remember that our net debt is now at 75 pe rcent of GDP, or $150 billion. So we will 
pay for these imports by borro wing or by selling more assets . That is the Government’s 
economic strategy. It is not a sustainable, long-term future for New Zealand. That is 
why we need to intervene on monetary policy, to bring the value of the dollar to a lower 
level so that our exporters can survive and compete from overseas, just like our trading 
nations are doing.  
The Green Party has put forw ard various proposals around that. Some of them are 
very much in line with the bill that we ha ve here today, which is  about changing some 
of the policy settings in terms of th e Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act. The 
International Monetary Fund in 2010 put out a paper about rethinking monetary policy. 
One of the key recommendations of that is that in small, open economies the central 
bank should target not just inflation but also the exchange rate. The reason it said that is 
that it recognises that sm all, open economies like ours ar e vulnerable to overvalued 
exchange rates that undermine the tradable sector and result in dramatic imbalances 
building up very quickly. That is why othe r small, open economies, like Switzerland, 
are intervening to bring down their dollar.  
This bill is a sensible bi ll. The Government is completely out of line with 
international best practice in supporting comp letely out-of-date monetary policy. It is 
time to move on. Thank you.
